Dagger linear logic for categorical quantum mechanics Thanks: Partially supported by NSERC, Canada
Robin Cockett \rsuper a, Cole Comfort \rsuper b, Priyaa V. Srinivasan \rsuper a

Abstract
. Categorical quantum mechanics exploits the dagger compact closed structure of finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, and uses the graphical calculus of string diagrams to facilitate reasoning about finite dimensional processes. A significant portion of quantum physics, however, involves reasoning about infinite dimensional processes, and it is well-known that the category of all Hilbert spaces is not compact closed. Thus, a limitation of using dagger compact closed categories is that one cannot directly accommodate reasoning about infinite dimensional processes. A natural categorical generalization of compact closed categories, in which infinite dimensional spaces can be modelled, is ∗ * -autonomous categories and, more generally, linearly distributive categories. This article starts the development of this direction of generalizing categorical quantum mechanics. An important first step is to establish the behaviour of the dagger in these more general settings. Thus, these notes simultaneously develop the categorical semantics of multiplicative dagger linear logic. The notes end with the definition of a mixed unitary category. It is this structure which is subsequently used to extend the key features of categorical quantum mechanics.

1.
Introduction

Categorical quantum mechanics (CQM), as described in
[
CK17
,
HJ19
]
, employs a graphical calculus for †-compact closed categories
(†-KCCs) to study quantum processes within the †-KCC of finite dimensional Hilbert spaces (
{\sf FHilb}
). From a logical perspective, the graphical calculus is
the proof theory of a compact fragment of multiplicative †-linear logic
[
Dun06
]
. This programme of CQM was initiated by Abramsky and Coecke’s seminal paper

[
AC04
]
and it has allowed much of the structure of
{\sf FHilb}
to be abstracted away and absorbed into the graphical calculus.

A well-known limitation of compact closed categories, is that, while they model finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, they do not model infinite dimensional
spaces
[
Heu08
]
. A categorical generalization of compact closed categories, in which infinite dimensions spaces can be modelled,
however, is *-autonomous categories. Thus, from a categorical perspective, an inviting direction to accommodate infinite dimensional
quantum processes is to utilize these *-autonomous settings as extensions of the compact closed settings of CQM. This can be taken a
step further by generalizing to linearly distributive categories (LDC) in which the existence of dual objects is not assumed. These linear
settings come with a proof theory – a graphical calculus – so that we need not abandon this key aspect of CQM. They also provide a
natural setting for Frobenius structures (see Egger
[
Egg10
]
), thus another important innovation of CQM can potentially be extended.
The downside is that these linear settings are more complicated as the single tensor product of CQM splits into two tensor products
(the tensor,
\otimes
, and the “par”,
\oplus
1
1

1

In the linear logic community the par is often written
\invamp
.
).

A first step towards extending CQM from compact closed categories to these linear settings is to understand how the dagger is expressed in

*
-autonomous and linearly distributive categories. This issue is the main focus of this paper. In CQM, the dagger structure directly
determines the important notion of a unitary isomorphism. As is discussed further below, the expression of unitary structure in linear
settings, is more complicated and leads ultimately to the introduction of mixed unitary categories (MUCs). A mixed unitary category may be
viewed as an essentially traditional CQM setting extended by a dagger linear setting in which (potentially) infinite dimensional objects can reside.
In our subsequent papers,
[
CS19a
,
CS19b
]
we show how some fundamental features of CQM can be realized in mixed unitary categories.
In
[
CS19a
]
we show, following the ideas in
[
CH16
]
, that completely positive maps can be expressed in mixed unitary categories and,
in
[
CS19b
]
, we explore Frobenius structure and complementarity in the mixed unitary setting.

The problem of extending CQM to include infinite dimensional processes has been explored in a number of different ways.
A fundamental feature of CQM is the replacement of the notion of an orthonormal basis by the algebraic structure of a special commutative

\dagger
-Frobenius algebra. In the category of finite dimensional Hilbert spaces the correspondence between orthonormal bases
and special commutative
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras is precise
[
CPV12
]
. Taking this correspondence as fundamental,
Abramsky and Heunen, in
[
AH12
]
, showed how Ambrose’s
H^{*}
-algebras
[
Amb45
]
could be used, in much the
same way, to replace orthonormal bases in infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces. However, there was a cost: they had to move
to semi-Frobenius algebras (that is they had to drop the units from the Frobenius structure) and to require a special property
(which they appropriately called
H^{*}
) on the maps from the unit. Gogoiso and Genovese
[
GG17
]
proposed an
interesting approach to reinstating the units using techniques from non-standard analysis
[
Rob96
]
.
They considered
~{}^{\star}
Hilb
the category of non-standard separable Hilbert Spaces and linear maps. This they claimed is a
dagger compact closed category, in which, among other things, the semi-Frobenius algebras of Abramsky and Heunen can be modelled.
Furthermore, the units can be reinstated because formal infinite sums are permitted.

In
[
CH16
]
, Coecke and Heunen, in order to include infinite dimensional quantum processes, take the simple step of dropping the
requirement of being compact closed and work in dagger symmetric monoidal categories (
\dagger
-SMCs). The category of Hilbert
spaces is the prototypical example of a
\dagger
-SMC. In particular, they show how to build, for an arbitrary
\dagger
-SMC, the
category of completely positive maps. Of course, it is also possible to consider special commutative
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras in an
arbitrary
\dagger
-SMC: although these, for Hilbert spaces are, of course, just the finite dimensional objects again. In
[
HR18
]
,
Heunen and Reyes considered a different
\dagger
-SMC, namely, the category of Hilbert
\mathbb{C}^{*}
-modules. Its objects can be equivalently viewed as
bundles of Hilbert spaces over a locally compact Hausdorff space. They characterized the special commutative
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras in this
category as bundles of finite dimensional Hilbert spaces (with dimensions are uniformly bounded). These objects, while being far from finite, do retain a
(uniform) locally finite nature. This example, by using vector bundles and ideas from differential geometry, enters the domain of traditional
theoretical physics, and serves as a reminder that
\dagger
-Frobenius algebras are not only of interest for Hilbert spaces.

The approach taken in this article to the problem of allowing infinite dimensional objects is different again. We accept CQM and its finite dimensionality as a
feature not a bug. However, we also accept that it is useful to have access to infinite dimensional structures. Rather than insisting that these infinite
dimensional structures are concretely related to Hilbert spaces, we allow that they may be a system of formal types which extend an essentially traditional
CQM core. A prototypical example of this is provided by the extension of finite dimensional complex matrices to infinite dimensional “finiteness matrices”
(see Example
3.5.2
).

The system of types extending the core are minimally expected to organize themselves into a linear setting with a dagger, that is, into a dagger
linearly distributive category (a
\dagger
-LDC). There are various reasons for this expectation. To start with the CQM core with its dagger involution is
already an example of a
\dagger
-LDC (albeit a “compact” one, that is one in which the two tensor products, tensor and par, coincide). Formally
extending such a CQM core with (infinite) limits and colimits freely – using the bicompletion of Joyal
[
Joy95
]
– causes the tensor product of the
core to separate into two linearly related tensor structures. These form the tensor,
\otimes
, and the par,
\oplus
, of linear logic and of a
\dagger
-LDC.
Extending a setting to accommodate infinite objects may, dually, be viewed as a process of extracting a core of “finite objects” from that larger setting.
Taking this latter view, suggests that we should start with a linear setting with a dagger, namely a
\dagger
-LDC, and extract from it a traditional CQM core.

At the very outset of such a program, there are some immediate – and perhaps paradigm breaking – questions to be faced. The most immediate one is the
question of what a
\dagger
-LDC might be. To answer this question is also to answer the question of what (multiplicative) “dagger linear logic” is.
This article essentially focuses on this question. It lays down the categorical groundwork for dagger linear logic and, thereby, begins to build a bridge to CQM.

Recall, following the lead of
[
AC04
,
Sel07
]
, that it is now standard in CQM to interpret the dagger functor as a stationary on objects
(A=A^{\dagger})
involution.
However, in the setting of linear logic and LDCs, one expects an involution to flip the tensor and par structure so that
A^{\dagger}\otimes B^{\dagger}=(A\oplus B)^{\dagger}
. This has
the – perhaps uncomfortable – effect of implying that, in these more general settings, the involution can no longer be viewed as being stationary on objects. Of course, having started
down this road, it seems prudent also to replace the equality above by a coherent isomorphism
\lambda_{\otimes}:A^{\dagger}\otimes B^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A\oplus B)^{\dagger}
and indeed the involution by an isomorphism
\iota_{A}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}
.

At this juncture it is perhaps appropriate to acknowledge that these are not new ideas. Models for quantum mechanics in
*
-autonomous categories are often described
as “toy models”
[
Abr12
]
and were, in particular discussed by Pavlovic
[
Pav11
]
where some very similar directions were advocated. Indeed, Egger
[
Egg11
]
, in initiating the
development of “involutive” categories, was also implicitly suggesting that dagger functors should not necessarily be regarded as being stationary on objects in these more
general settings. Section
4
is essentially a realization of Egger’s ideas: we have, however, changed his terminology preferring to talk of “conjugation”
rather than “involution” as we think of the contravariant dagger,
(\_)^{\dagger}
, as an involution. Nonetheless, conjugation and involution are closely related (see section
4
) as in the presence of dualization having conjugation is equivalent to having an involution.

There are some significant complications attendant on allowing a non-stationary dagger. The first and foremost amongst these is that
one gets inundated by coherence issues. This article does provide a path through these coherence issues, and, hopefully shows – once one has assimilated all
the structure – that these issues are not nearly as terrible as might be expected. However, we are forced to concede that they are non-trivial. The next problem,
once the coherences are under control, is that one would like to be able to say what a unitary isomorphism is with respect to a non-stationary involution. How
this may be accomplished seems, at first glance, less than obvious.

The fact that the dagger functor is an involution with a coherent isomorphism
\iota_{A}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}
makes it natural to view a

unitary object
as an object with an isomorphism
\varphi_{A}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
, such that
\iota_{A}=\varphi_{A}(\varphi_{A}^{-1})^{\dagger}
: we refer to
\varphi_{A}
as
the
unitary structure
of
A
. Considering this, with the expected coherent behaviour of this unitary structure, leads one to realize that, for unitary objects, we
must also have
A\otimes B\simeq A\oplus B
. This, in turn, leads one to ask how this can happen in an LDC. Fortunately, there is a theory which has been developed
for this situation: namely that of LDCs with mix
[
CS97b
,
Pav11
]
. An LDC with mix has a coherent map, from the par unit to the tensor unit
{\sf m}:\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\top
, called the
mix map
, which, in turn, induces a map
{\sf mx}:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus B
, called the
mixor
. In a mix category we say an object
A
is in the
core

[
BCS00
]
in case the mixor for that object with any other object,
{\sf mx}_{A,X}:A\otimes X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus X
, is an isomorphism. This allows our earlier expectation to be expressed as the requirement that unitary objects be in the core. As
\dagger
-LDCs with mix play an important role in this development we refer to them as a
\dagger
-mix category. If, further, we want our unitary objects to form a
compact
LDC – that is one in which the tensor and par structures are equivalent – then the tensor and par structures must agree at their units, which means we must ask that the mix map,
{\sf m}:\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\top
, be an isomorphism. The first milestone of the paper is therefore to collect all this structure into what we call a
\dagger
-isomix category
.

Amidst the introduction of all this structure, the astute reader may notice that we have still failed to elucidate how the unitary isomorphisms arise. Let us hasten to correct
this oversight: a unitary isomorphism
f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
is an isomorphism between unitary objects which is (twisted) natural with respect to the unitary structures,
\varphi_{A}
and
\varphi_{B}
2
2

2

This formulation of unitary isomorphisms is not completely original as a lively discussion of whether
\dagger
-categories were “evil” led
Peter Lumsdaine to suggest in the math overflow forum
[
LL15
]
how they might be made a little less evil. These ideas never took off, perhaps because it was pointed
out by Peter Selinger that, when one regarded something as evil if it was not preserved by equivalence, then it was impossible for dagger not to be evil! Here we quite explicitly
have “unitary structure” which is of course is not only not necessarily unique but also will not necessarily be preserved by an equivalence. Thus, like all structure, it is thoroughly evil!
,
in the sense that the following diagram is rendered commutative:

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\scriptstyle{f}
\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{B}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f^{\dagger}}

Note that, when the unitary structure is the identity map, we recover the usual notion of unitary isomorphism.
The coherence requirements on unitary structure then have the pleasing effect of forcing the coherence isomorphisms, for unitary objects,
to be unitary maps.

A
unitary category
is a
\dagger
-isomix category in which
all
objects have a unitary structure. Unitary categories are necessarily compact LDCs and so are rather special.
In fact, we show that they are
\dagger
-linearly equivalent to the more standard CQM notion of a
\dagger
-SMC – and, furthermore, that a closed
unitary category is linearly equivalent to a dagger compact closed category,
\dagger
-KCC. One may – with some justification – feel that one has, at this stage, come full circle as the standard structures from categorical quantum mechanics seem to be emerging. However, notice that it is our more complex notion of unitary that allows the extraction of a unitary core from a larger
\dagger
-isomix category: the larger
\dagger
-isomix category, with its possibly infinite dimensional objects, is still available.

A mixed unitary category (MUC) is a strong
\dagger
-isomix functor
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
, which has domain a “small” unitary category (the unitary core) and codomain of a “large”
\dagger
-isomix category.
A mixed unitary category can be represented schematically as follows:

A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.43474pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\varphi_{A}$}}_{\hbox{\scriptsize$\simeq$}}}A^{\dagger}
Unitary
category
\dagger
-isomix
functor
\dagger
-isomix
category
B
B^{\dagger}

One may think of the unitary category as acting on the larger category, much as a field
K
acts on a
K
-algebra as scalars.
Expressing these categories in this manner allows an obvious notion of functor as a square of
\dagger
-Frobenius functors, whose component on the unitary categories preserves unitary structure, and which commutes up to a linear natural isomorphism.
For any
\dagger
-isomix category one can build a unitary category by collecting the “pre-unitary” objects which are in the core. This give a way of generating a mixed unitary category from a
\dagger
-isomix category, which we call the unitary construction.

We have provided examples throughout the text. An important example, closely related to traditional CQM, is the
*
-autonomous category of “finiteness matrices”,
{\sf FMat}(\mathbb{C})
, over the complex numbers
[
Ehr05
]
(see Example
3.5.2
). Here the maps are infinite dimensional matrices whose support is carefully controlled by the finiteness structure. The dagger on the category is given by simultaneously transposing and conjugating the matrices: on objects it is given by taking the dual finiteness space.
{\sf FMat}(\mathbb{C})
forms a
\dagger
-isomix category which, furthermore, is
\dagger
-
*
-autonomous. An object is in the core if and only if it’s underlying finiteness space is finite and these objects are also exactly the unitary objects. The unitary structure of a finite object in this case is the identity map (so the unitary structure is “trivial”) – which means that the coherence requirements are immediately satisfied.

Another source of examples (see Example
4.4.2
) is from the Chu construction,
[
Bar06
]
, where the dualizing object is set to the tensor unit. Considering the Chu construction over complex vector spaces there is an obvious notion of conjugation which means that this category forms a
\dagger
-isomix category. From there one can obtain a non-trivial MUC by extracting the pre-unitary objects, or, more directly, by using the fact that the category of Hilbert spaces embeds into this category. To obtain a MUC one must then restrict this last embedding to the finite dimensional Hilbert spaces.

Notation:

Throughout the paper we use diagrammatic order for composition of maps so
fg:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}C=A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.68407pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f$}}}B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.15244pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$g$}}}C
. Functors, however, are usually written using applicative notation so that
GF(A)=F(G(A))
. We write par, the dual linear logic tensor, as
\oplus
throughout. Circuit diagrams should be read from top to bottom (in the same direction as the pull of gravity).

2.
Linearly distributive categories

This section recalls some background concepts from the theory of linearly distributive categories. The definition of linearly distributive categories is available in
[
CS97b
,
BCST96
]
. Here we briefly recall the definition of linear functors and their transformations
[
CS99
]
, the notion of a linear adjoint
[
CKS00
]
– which we shall refer to as a linear dual – and the notion of a mix category and its core
[
CS97a
,
BCS00
]
.

2.1.
Linearly distributive categories, functors, and transformations

A
linearly distributive category (LDC)
is a category,
\mathbb{X}
, with two monoidal structures

(\otimes,\top,a_{\otimes},u_{\otimes}^{L},u_{\otimes}^{R})~~~\mbox{ and }~~~(\oplus,\bot,a_{\oplus},u_{\oplus}^{L},u_{\oplus}^{R})

linked by natural transformations called the linear distributors:

\displaystyle\partial^{L}:A\otimes(B\oplus C)\rightarrow(A\otimes B)\oplus C

\displaystyle\partial^{R}:(B\oplus C)\otimes A\rightarrow B\oplus(C\otimes A)

such that the monoidal natural isomorphisms - associators and unitors - interact coherently with the linear distributors, see
[
BCST96
,
CS97b
]
for more details. A symmetric LDC is an LDC in which both monoidal structures are symmetric, with symmetry maps
c_{\otimes}
and
c_{\oplus}
, such that

\partial^{R}=c_{\otimes}(1\otimes c_{\oplus})\partial^{L}(c_{\otimes}\oplus 1)c_{\oplus}
.

LDCs provide categorical semantics for the multiplicative linear logic (MLL). LDCs come equipped with a graphical calculus
[
BCST96
]
that contains the calculus for monoidal categories.

In this section, we review the fundamentals of the graphical calculus for LDCs. For detailed exposition, see
[
BCST96
,
CS97b
]
.
The following are the generators of LDC circuits: wires represent objects and circles represent maps. The input wires of a map are tensored (with
\otimes
), and the output wires are “par”ed (with
\oplus
). The following diagram represents a map
f:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}C\oplus D
.

f
A
B
C
D
f:A\oplus B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}C\otimes D

\otimes
-associator, the
\oplus
-associator, the left linear distributor, and the right linear distributors are, respectively, drawn as follows:

As in linear logic, not all circuit diagrams constructed from these basic components represent a valid LDC circuit. In his seminal paper on linear logic,
[
Gir87
]
, Girard introduced a criterion for the correctness of his representation of proofs using proof nets based on switching links. A valid proof structure must be connected and acyclic for all the switching link choices. Using this correctness criterion has the disadvantage of requiring exponential time in the number of switching links. Danos and Regnier
[
DR89
]
improved this situation significantly by providing an algorithm for correctness which takes linear time (see
[
Gue99
]
)
on the size of the circuit. To verify the validity of the circuit diagrams of LDCs, Blute et.al.
[
BCST96
]
, provided a boxing algorithm which was based on Danos and Regnier’s more efficient algorithm which we now describe.

In order to verify that an LDC circuit is valid, circuit components are “boxed” using the below rules. The primitive generating maps are
automatically boxed.

Double lines refer to multiple number of wires.
\otimes
-introduction and
\oplus
-elimination are boxed in
(a_{1})
and
(a_{2})
respectively. In
(b_{1})
, it is shown how a box ‘eats’ the
\otimes
-elimination: in
(b_{2})
the dual rule shows a
\oplus
-introduction being eaten.
(c)
shows how boxes can be amalgamated when they are connected by a single wire. In
(e_{1})
-
(e_{4})
, it is shown how the thinning links can be boxed. By progressively enclosing the components of the circuit in boxes using these rules, if we end up with a single box (or a wire), precisely when the circuit is valid.

In the firts step the
\otimes
-introduction and
\oplus
-elimination are boxed. In the second step the boxes are amalgamated along the single wire joining them. In the third step, the box absorbs the
\otimes
-elimination and
\oplus
-introduction.

Before presenting the definition of linear functors, we briefly recall the definition of monoidal functors.
A functor
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
between monoidal categories is a monoidal functor if it is equipped with natural transformations
m_{\otimes}:F(A)\otimes F(B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F(A\otimes B)
and
m_{I}:I\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F(I)
such that the following diagrams commute:

\textstyle{(F(A)\otimes F(B))\otimes F(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}\otimes 1}
\textstyle{F(A\otimes B)\otimes F(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F((A\otimes B)\otimes C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F(a_{\otimes})}
\textstyle{F(A)\otimes(F(B)\otimes F(C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(A)\otimes F(B\otimes C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(A\otimes(B\otimes C))}

\textstyle{F(A)\otimes I\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\otimes}^{R}}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes m_{I}}
\textstyle{F(A)\otimes F(I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(A\otimes I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F(u_{\otimes}^{L})}
\textstyle{F(A)}

\textstyle{I\otimes F(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\otimes}^{L}}
\scriptstyle{m_{I}\otimes 1}
\textstyle{F(I)\otimes F(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(I\otimes A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F(u_{\otimes}^{L})}
\textstyle{F(A)}

The first diagram for the monoidal functor is the associative law, and the other two diagrams are the right and the left unit laws respectively.

{defi}

[
CS99
, Definition 1]

Given linearly distributive categories
\mathbb{X}
and
\mathbb{Y}
, a linear functor
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
consists of

(1)

a pair of functors
F=(F_{\otimes},F_{\oplus})
:
(F_{\otimes},m_{\otimes},m_{\top})
which is monoidal with respect to
\otimes
and
(F_{\oplus},n_{\oplus},n_{\bot})
which is comonoidal with respect to
\oplus
. We refer to
m_{\otimes}
and
n_{\oplus}
as
tensor laxors
, and
m_{\top}
and
n_{\bot}
as
unit laxors
.

(2)

natural transformations:

\displaystyle\nu_{\otimes}^{R}

\displaystyle:F_{\otimes}(A\oplus B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\otimes}(B)

\displaystyle\nu_{\otimes}^{L}

\displaystyle:F_{\otimes}(A\oplus B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\otimes}(A)\oplus F_{\oplus}(B)

\displaystyle\nu_{\oplus}^{R}

\displaystyle:F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes F_{\oplus}(B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A\otimes B)

\displaystyle\nu_{\oplus}^{L}

\displaystyle:F_{\oplus}(A)\otimes F_{\otimes}(B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A\otimes B)

such that the following coherence conditions hold:

]

(1)

(a)

F_{\otimes}(u^{L}_{\oplus})=\nu^{R}_{\otimes}(n_{\bot}\oplus 1)u^{L}_{\oplus}

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(\bot\oplus A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(u_{\oplus}^{L})}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(\bot)\oplus F_{\otimes}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\bot}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{\bot\oplus F_{\otimes}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\oplus}^{L}}

(b)

\nu_{\otimes}^{L}(1\oplus n_{\bot})u_{\oplus}^{R}=F_{\otimes}(u_{\oplus}^{R})

(c)

(u_{\otimes}^{L})^{-1}(m_{\top}\otimes 1)\nu_{\oplus}^{R}=F_{\oplus}((u_{\otimes}^{L})^{-1})

(d)

(u_{\otimes}^{R})^{-1}(m_{\top}\otimes 1)\nu_{\oplus}^{L}=F_{\oplus}((u_{\otimes}^{R})^{-1})

(2)

(a)

F_{\otimes}(a_{\oplus})\nu^{R}_{\otimes}(1\oplus\nu^{R}_{\otimes})=\nu^{R}_{\otimes}(n_{\oplus}\oplus 1)a_{\oplus}

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}((A\oplus B)\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(a_{\oplus})}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(a_{\oplus})}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A\oplus(B\oplus C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A\oplus B)\oplus F_{\otimes}(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\otimes}(B\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{(F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\oplus}(B))\oplus F_{\otimes}(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus(F_{\oplus}(B)\oplus F_{\oplus}(C))}

(b)

F_{\otimes}(a_{\oplus})\nu_{\otimes}^{L}(1\oplus n_{\oplus})=\nu^{L}_{\oplus}(\nu^{L}\oplus 1)a_{\oplus}

(c)

(m_{\otimes}\otimes 1)\nu_{\oplus}^{R}F_{\oplus}(a_{\otimes})=a_{\otimes}(1\otimes\nu_{\oplus}^{R})\nu_{\oplus}^{R}

(d)

(\nu^{R}_{\oplus}\otimes 1)\nu_{\oplus}^{L}F_{\oplus}(a_{\otimes})=a_{\otimes}(1\otimes m_{\otimes})\nu_{\oplus}^{L}

(3)

(a)

F_{\otimes}(a_{\oplus})\nu^{R}_{\otimes}(1\oplus\nu^{L}_{\otimes})=\nu_{\otimes}^{L}(\nu^{R}_{\otimes}\oplus 1)a_{\oplus}

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}((A\oplus B)\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(a_{\oplus})}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{L}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A\oplus(B\oplus C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A\oplus B)\oplus F_{\oplus}(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\otimes}(B\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\nu_{\otimes}^{L}}
\textstyle{(F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\otimes}(B))\oplus F_{\oplus}(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus(F_{\otimes}(B)\oplus F_{\oplus}(C))}

(b)

(\nu^{R}_{\oplus}\otimes 1)\nu^{L}_{\oplus}F_{\oplus}(a_{\otimes})=a_{\otimes}(1\otimes\nu_{\oplus}^{L})\nu_{\oplus}^{R}

(4)

(a)

(1\otimes\nu^{R}_{\otimes})\partial^{L}(\nu^{R}_{\oplus}\oplus 1)=m_{\otimes}F_{\otimes}(\partial^{L})\nu^{R}_{\otimes}

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes F_{\otimes}(B\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes(F_{\oplus}(B)\oplus F_{\otimes}(C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial^{L}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A\otimes(B\oplus C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(\partial^{L})}
\textstyle{(F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes F_{\oplus}(B))\oplus F_{\otimes}(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\oplus}^{R}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}((A\otimes B)\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A\oplus B)\oplus F_{\otimes}(C)}

(b)

(\nu_{\otimes}^{L}\otimes 1)\partial^{R}(1\oplus\nu_{\oplus}^{L})=m_{\otimes}F_{\otimes}(\partial^{R})\nu_{\otimes}^{L}

(c)

(1\otimes\nu_{\otimes}^{L})\partial^{L}(\nu_{\oplus}^{L}\oplus 1)=\nu_{\oplus}^{L}F_{\oplus}(\partial^{L})n_{\oplus}

(d)

(\nu_{\otimes}^{R}\otimes 1)\partial^{R}(1\oplus\nu_{\oplus}^{R})=\nu_{\oplus}^{R}F_{\oplus}(\partial^{R})n_{\oplus}

(5)

(a)

(1\otimes\nu^{L}_{\otimes})\partial^{L}(m_{\otimes}\oplus 1)=m_{\otimes}F_{\otimes}(\partial^{L})\nu^{L}_{\otimes}

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes F_{\otimes}(B\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\nu_{\otimes}^{L}}

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes(F_{\otimes}(B)\oplus F_{\oplus}(C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}((A\otimes B)\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{L}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A\otimes B)\oplus F_{\oplus}(C)}

(b)

(\nu_{\otimes}^{R}\otimes 1)\partial^{R}(1\oplus m_{\otimes})=m_{\otimes}F_{\otimes}(\partial^{R})\nu_{\otimes}^{R}

(c)

(1\otimes n_{\oplus})\partial^{L}(\nu_{\oplus}^{R}\oplus 1)=\nu_{\oplus}^{R}F_{\oplus}(\partial^{L})n_{\oplus}

(d)

(n_{\oplus}\otimes 1)\partial^{R}(1\oplus\nu_{\oplus}^{L})=\nu_{\oplus}^{L}F_{\oplus}(\partial^{R})n_{\oplus}

In the graphical calculus, functors are represented by linear functor boxes
[
CS99
]
. A linear functor box can be monoidal or comonoidal. When the functor box is monoidal
(F_{\otimes})
, it has one principal output wire (represented by a port where the wire exits the box) and the other wires are auxiliary. When the box is comonoidal (
F_{\oplus}
), it has one principal input wire with a port and the other wires are auxiliary. The functor boxes are subject to a very natural “box eats box” calculus described in
[
CS99
]
. A box can eat another box only when a ported wire meets an auxiliary wire.

When working in the categorical doctrine of
symmetric
LDCs we will expect the linear functors to preserve the symmetry. Thus, a
symmetric linear functor
is a linear functor
F=(F_{\otimes},F_{\oplus})

which satisfies in addition:

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes F_{\otimes}(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{c_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A\otimes B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(c_{\otimes})}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(B)\otimes F_{\otimes}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(B\otimes A)}

\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F_{\oplus}(c_{\oplus})}
\scriptstyle{n_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\oplus}(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{c_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(B\otimes A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(B)\oplus F_{\oplus}(A)}

Natural transformations between linear functors also break into two components linking respectively the tensor functors and, in the opposite direction, the par functors:

{defi}

[
CS99
, Definition 3]

A
linear (natural) transformation
,
\alpha:F\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G
, between parallel linear functors
F,G:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
consists of a pair of natural transformations
\alpha=(\alpha_{\otimes},\alpha_{\oplus})
such that
\alpha_{\otimes}:F_{\otimes}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G_{\otimes}
is a monoidal transformation and
\alpha_{\oplus}:G_{\oplus}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}
is a comonoidal transformation satisfying the following coherence conditions:

]

(1)

a_{\otimes}\nu^{R}_{\otimes}(a_{\oplus}\oplus 1)=\nu^{R}_{\otimes}(1\oplus a_{\otimes})

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{G_{\otimes}(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\nu_{\otimes}^{R}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\otimes}(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\alpha_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{G_{\oplus}(A)\oplus G_{\otimes}(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\oplus}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus G_{\otimes}(B)}

(2)

\alpha_{\otimes}\nu_{\otimes}^{L}(1\oplus\alpha_{\oplus})=\nu_{\otimes}^{L}(\alpha_{\otimes}\oplus 1)

(3)

(1\otimes\alpha_{\otimes})\nu_{\oplus}^{L}(\alpha_{\oplus})=(\alpha_{\oplus}\otimes 1)\nu_{\oplus}^{L}

(4)

(\alpha_{\otimes}\otimes 1)\nu_{\oplus}^{R}\alpha_{\oplus}=(1\otimes\alpha_{\oplus})\nu_{\oplus}^{R}

An adjunction of linear functors,
(\eta,\epsilon):F\dashv G
is an adjunction in the usual sense
(i.e. satisfying the triangle equalities) in the 2-category of LDCs with linear functors and
linear natural transformations. In particular, such an adjunction yields a pair of
adjunctions:
(\eta_{\otimes},\epsilon_{\otimes}):F_{\otimes}\dashv G_{\otimes}
which is a monoidal adjunction,
and
(\epsilon_{\oplus},\eta_{\oplus}):G_{\oplus}\dashv F_{\oplus}
which is a comonoidal adjunction.
By Kelly’s results
[
Kel74
]
, a functor with a right adjoint is comonoidal if and only if its
right adjoint is monoidal. This leads to the observation that:

Lemma 1
.

If
(\eta,\epsilon):F\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv G
is an adjunction of linear functors, then
F_{\otimes}
is iso-monoidal (or strong) with respect to
\otimes
and
F_{\oplus}
is iso-comonoidal making the
linear functor
F
strong.

Proof 2.1
.

Since
(\eta_{\otimes},\epsilon_{\otimes}):F_{\otimes}\dashv G_{\otimes}
is a monoidal adjunction, the left adjoint
(F_{\otimes},m_{\otimes},m_{\top})
is a strong monoidal functor. Similarly, since
(\epsilon_{\oplus},\eta_{\oplus}):G_{\oplus}\dashv F_{\oplus}
is a comonoidal adjunction, the right adjoint
(F_{\oplus},n_{\oplus},n_{\bot})
is a strong comonoidal functor.

A
linear equivalence
is a linear adjunction in which the unit and counit are linear natural isomorphisms.

2.2.
Mix categories

In this paper we shall be predominately concerned with LDCs which have a mix map:

{defi}

[
CS97a
]

An LDC is a
mix category
in case there is a
mix map

{\sf m}:\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\top
in
\mathbb{X}
such that:

\textstyle{A\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes u_{\oplus}^{L^{-1}}}
\scriptstyle{(u_{\oplus}^{R})^{-1}\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}_{A,B}}
\textstyle{A\otimes(\bot\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes({\sf m}\oplus 1)}
\textstyle{A\otimes(\top\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial^{L}}
\textstyle{(A\oplus\bot)\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial^{R}}
\textstyle{(A\otimes\top)\oplus B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\otimes}^{R}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{A\oplus(\bot\otimes B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus({\sf m}\otimes 1)}
\textstyle{A\oplus(\top\otimes B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus u_{\otimes}^{L}}
\textstyle{A\oplus B}

The map
\mathsf{mx}_{A,B}
is natural and is called the
mixor
. The coherence condition for the mix map has the following form in string diagrams (where the mix map is represented by an empty box):

In a mix category, the associator, the distributor and the mix maps interact as follows. See Lemma 2, and proposition 3 in
[
BCS00
]
for a proof.

[mix.]

\textstyle{(A\oplus B)\otimes C\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\delta^{R}}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
\scriptstyle{(a)}
\textstyle{A\oplus(B\otimes C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\mathsf{mx}}
\textstyle{(A\oplus B)\oplus C\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{A\oplus(B\oplus C)}

\textstyle{(A\otimes B)\otimes C\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
\scriptstyle{a_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{(b)}
\textstyle{A\oplus(B\otimes C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\delta^{L}}
\textstyle{A\otimes(B\otimes C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\mathsf{mx}}
\textstyle{A\otimes(B\oplus C)}

\textstyle{C\otimes(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\delta^{L}}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
\scriptstyle{(c)}
\textstyle{(C\otimes A)\oplus B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{C\oplus(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\oplus}^{-1}}
\textstyle{(C\oplus A)\oplus B}

\textstyle{A\otimes(B\otimes C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}

\scriptstyle{(d)}
\textstyle{A\oplus(B\otimes C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{(A\oplus B)\otimes C}

There are many examples of mix categories including Coherence spaces
[
Gir87
]
,
and Finiteness spaces
[
Ehr05
]
.

When the mix map
{\sf m}
is an isomorphism, then
\mathbb{X}
is said to be an
isomix category
.
Recall that, when
{\sf m}
is an isomorphism, the coherence requirement for the mixor is
automatically satisfied (see
[
CS97a
, Lemma 6.6]
). Finiteness spaces
[
Ehr05
]
and Chu Spaces
[
Bar06
]

provide examples of isomix categories.

An isomix category,
(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
always has two linear functors
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}:(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\otimes)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
and
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}:(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\oplus)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)

given by the identity functor, that is
({\sf Mx}_{\uparrow})_{\otimes}=({\sf Mx}_{\uparrow})_{\oplus}={\sf Id}=({\sf Mx}_{\downarrow})_{\otimes}=({\sf Mx}_{\downarrow})_{\oplus}
.
The linear strengths and monoidal maps are given by the inverse of the mix map and the mixor.
These mix functors take the degenerate linear structure on the tensor (respectively the par)
and spread it out over both the tensor structures.

Lemma 2
.

For any isomix category
\mathbb{X}
the functors
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}:(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\otimes)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)

and
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}:(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\oplus)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
are linear functors.

Proof 2.2
.

We show that
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}:(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\otimes)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
is a linear functor:
the monoidal and comonoidal components of the functor are given by

(1,1,1)
and
(1,\mathsf{mx},{\sf m}^{-1})
respectively. The linear strenghts are
\nu_{\otimes}^{L}=\nu_{\otimes}^{R}:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus B:=\mathsf{mx}
and
\nu_{\oplus}^{L}=\nu_{\oplus}^{R}:A\oplus B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus B:=1
.

First we show
(1,\mathsf{mx},{\sf m}^{-1}):(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\otimes)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
is a monoidal functor:

•

The associative law for monoidal functors,
(\mathsf{mx}\otimes 1)~\mathsf{mx}~a_{\oplus}=a_{\otimes}~(1\otimes\mathsf{mx})~\mathsf{mx}
,
is satisfied:

•

The unit laws for monoidal functors hold. Here is the pictorial proof of
(1\otimes{\sf m}^{-1})\mathsf{mx}=u_{\otimes}^{L}(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}
, where
the filled rectangles represent
{\sf m}^{-1}
:

[LF.4]
(b) - (d) and
[LF.5]
(a) - (d) are satisfied similarly.

Thus,
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}
is a linear functor.

The proof that
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}
is a linear functor is (linearly) dual.

In fact, these linear functors and are examples of
isomix Frobenius functors
,
which we shall introduce formally in the Section
3.1
.

2.3.
Compact LDCs

A
compact LDC
is an isomix category in which each mixor
\mathsf{mx}_{A,B}
is an isomorphism.
An important way in which compact LDCs arise is from the “core” of an isomix category:

{defi}

[
BCS00
]

The
core
of a mix category,
\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})\subseteq\mathbb{X}
, is the full subcategory with objects
U
such that the mixors

U\otimes(\_)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to33.57147pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\mathsf{mx}_{U,(\_)}$}}}U\oplus(\_)~~~~\mbox{and}~~~~(\_)\otimes U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to34.01591pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\mathsf{mx}_{(\_),U}$}}}(\_)\oplus U

are isomorphisms.

Proposition 3
.

[
BCS00
, Proposition 3]

If
\mathbb{X}
is a mix-LDC and
A,B\in\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
then
A\oplus B
and
A\otimes B\in\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
(and
A\oplus B\simeq A\otimes B
). If
\mathbb{X}
is an isomix-LDC, then
\top,\bot\in\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
.

Corollary 4
.

When
\mathbb{X}
is a compact LDC, the mix functors,
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}
and
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}
, are linear isomorphisms. Consequently, compact LDCs are linearly equivalent to monoidal categories.

We shall denote the inverse of
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}
by

{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\downarrow}:(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\oplus)
: this is the identity functor as a mere functor,
strict on the par structure, and on the tensor structure having as the unit laxor
{\sf m}
and as the tensor laxor
{\sf mx}^{-1}
. Similarly, we shall denote the inverse of
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}
by
{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}
.

2.4.
Linear duals

A key notion in the theory of LDCs is the notion of a linear adjoint
[
CKS00
]
. Here we shall refer to linear adjoints as “linear duals” in order to avoid any confusion with an adjunction of linear functors.

{defi}

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
is a LDC and
A,B\in\mathbb{X}
, then
B
is
left linear dual
(or left linear adjoint) to
A
– or
A
is
right linear dual
(right linear adjoint) to
B
– written
(\eta,\epsilon):B\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
, if there exists
\eta:\top\rightarrow B\oplus A
and
\epsilon:A\otimes B\rightarrow\bot
such that the following diagrams commute:

\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(u_{\otimes}^{L})^{-1}}
\textstyle{\top\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\eta\otimes 1}
\textstyle{(B\oplus A)\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial_{R}}
\textstyle{B}
\textstyle{B\oplus\bot\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\oplus}^{R}}
\textstyle{B\oplus(A\otimes B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\epsilon}

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(u_{\otimes}^{R})^{-1}}
\textstyle{A\otimes\top\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\eta}
\textstyle{A\otimes(B\oplus A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial_{L}}
\textstyle{A}
\textstyle{\bot\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\oplus}^{L}}
\textstyle{(A\otimes B)\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\epsilon\oplus 1}

The commuting diagrams are called often referred to as “snake diagrams” because of their shape when drawn in string calculus:

Lemma 5
.

[
BCS00
]

(1)

In an LDC if
(\eta,\epsilon):B\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
and
(\eta^{\prime},\epsilon^{\prime}):C\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
, then
B
and
C
are isomorphic;

(2)

In a symmetric LDC
(\eta,\epsilon):B\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
if and only if
(\eta c_{\oplus},c_{\otimes}\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
;

(3)

In a mix-LDC if
B\in\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
and
B\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
, then
A\in\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
.

Lemma 6
.

[
CKS00
]

Linear functors preserve linear duals: when
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
is a linear functor and
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B\in\mathbb{X}
, then
F_{\otimes}(A)\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv F_{\oplus}(B)
and
F_{\oplus}(A)\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv F_{\otimes}(B)
.

The unit and counit of the other adjunction is given similarly, however using the right linear strengths (
\nu_{\otimes}^{R}
and
\nu_{\oplus}^{R}
).

An LDC in which every object has a chosen left and right linear dual, respectively
(\eta{*},\epsilon{*}):A^{*}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
and
({*}\eta,{*}\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv\!~^{*}A
, is a
*
-autonomous category
. In the symmetric case a left linear dual gives a right linear dual using the symmetry: thus, it is standard to assume the existence of just the left dual with the right being the same object with the unit and counit given by symmetry (as above).

Just as compact LDCs are linearly equivalent to monoidal categories so compact
*
-autonomous categories are linearly equivalent to compact closed categories. The equivalence is given by
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}
which spreads the par onto two tensor structures (or, indeed, by
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}
which shows how to spread out a compact closed
structure on the tensor).

In a symmetric
*
-autonomous category the left dual of an object is always canonically isomorphic to the right dual. Moreover, even in non-symmetric
*
-autonomous categories, it is often the case that the two duals are coherently isomorphic:

{defi}

[
EM12
]

A
cyclor
in a
*
-autonomous category
(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot,~^{*}(\_),(\_)^{*})

*
-autonomous categories always have a canonical cyclor:

*\eta
\epsilon*
A^{*}

We shall use the cyclor in Section
4
to show how conjugation and dagger are related in the presence of dualization.

3.
Frobenius functors and daggers

We shall be interested here in linear functors between LDCs called Frobenius functors
which come in various flavours, including mix functors and isomix functors,
as illustrated in Figure
1
. These functors are directly related
to the Frobenius monoidal functors of
[
DP08
]
and they are referred to as degenerate
linear functors in
[
BPS12
]
. Furthermore, we have already seen two rather basic examples,
namely,
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}
and
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}
.

Linear functors
Frobenius functors
Mix functors
Isomix functors
(Normal functors)
m_{\top}F({\sf m}^{-1})n_{\bot}={\sf m}^{-1}
n_{\bot}{\sf m}m_{\top}=F({\sf m})
F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus};m_{\otimes}=\nu_{\oplus}^{L}=\nu_{\oplus}^{R};n_{\oplus}=\nu_{\otimes}^{L}=\nu_{\otimes}^{R}
cyclic functors
symmetric functors

Figure 1.
Linear functor family

Frobenius functors preserve linear duals and with an additional coherence condition they preserve the mix map. The coherence requirements for a dagger on an LDC are implied by requiring that the dagger functor be a Frobenius involutive equivalence. Once the dagger is understood we can consider
\dagger
-mix categories and their functors which we shall take to be mix Frobenius functors with a further requirement concerning the preservation of the dagger.

3.1.
Frobenius functors

{defi}

A
Frobenius functor
is a linear functor
F
such that:

]

(1)

F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus}

(2)

m_{\otimes}=\nu_{\oplus}^{R}=\nu_{\oplus}^{L}

(3)

n_{\oplus}=\nu_{\otimes}^{L}=\nu_{\otimes}^{R}

The left and right linear strengths of
\otimes
and
\oplus
coinciding with the
m_{\otimes}
and
n_{\oplus}
respectively means that in the diagrammatic calculus, ports can be moved around freely:

A Frobenius functor is
symmetric
if as a linear functor it preserves the symmetries of the tensor and par.

Lemma 7
.

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
and
\mathbb{Y}
are LDCs. The following are equivalent:

(1)

F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
is a Frobenius linear functor.

(2)

F
is
\otimes
-monoidal and
\oplus
-comonoidal such that

\scriptstyle{1\otimes n_{\oplus}}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}

\textstyle{F(A)\otimes(F(B)\oplus F(C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial^{L}}
\textstyle{F(A\otimes(B\oplus C))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F(\partial^{L})}
\textstyle{(F(A)\otimes F(B))\oplus F(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F((A\oplus B)\oplus C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F(A\oplus B)\oplus F(C)}

\textstyle{F(A\oplus B)\otimes F(C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

Proof 3.1
.

For (a)
\Rightarrow
(b), fix
F:=F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus}
, then
F
is
\otimes
-monoidal and
\oplus
-comonoidal. Conditions
[F.1]
and
[F.2]
are given by
[LF.5]-(a)
and
[LF.5]-(b)
. For the other direction, define
F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus}:=F
. Then it is straightforward to check that all the axioms of Frobenius linear functors are satisfied by
(F_{\otimes},F_{\oplus})
.

Frobenius functors compose: the composition is defined as the usual composition of linear functors
[
CS97b
]
.

It is immediate from Lemma
6
that Frobenius functors preserve linear duals. In fact if
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
is a Frobenius functor
and
A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B
is a linear dual, as the duals
F_{\otimes}(A)\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv F_{\oplus}(B)
and
F_{\oplus}(A)\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv F_{\otimes}(B)
now coincide, we just obtain the
one dual
F(A)\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv F(B)
. In the case when the Frobenius functor is between cyclic
*
-autonomous categories we expect the
functor to be
cyclor-preserving
in the following sense:

[CFF]

\textstyle{F(X^{*})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\cong}
\scriptstyle{F(\psi)}
\textstyle{F(\!\!~^{*}X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\cong}
\textstyle{F(X)^{*}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi}
\textstyle{\!\!~{}^{*}F(X)}

where the left and right vertical arrows are respectively the maps:

(u^{R}_{\otimes})^{-1}(\eta*\otimes 1)\partial^{R}(1\oplus(m^{F}_{\otimes}F(\epsilon*)n^{F}_{\bot}))u^{R}_{\oplus}~~~\mbox{and}~~~(u^{R})^{-1}(1\otimes*\eta)\partial^{L}(m^{F}_{\otimes}\oplus 1)((F(*\epsilon)n_{\bot}^{F})\oplus 1)u^{L}_{\oplus}

Linear natural isomorphisms between Frobenius functors
(\alpha_{\otimes},\alpha_{\oplus}):F\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G
often take a special form with
\alpha_{\otimes}=\alpha_{\oplus}^{-1}
: this allows the coherence
requirements to be simplified. The next results describe some basic circumstances in which this happens:

Lemma 10
.

Suppose
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
, and
G:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
are Frobenius linear functors and
\alpha:=(\alpha_{\otimes},\alpha_{\oplus}):F\Rightarrow G
is a linear natural transformation. Then, the following are equivalent:

(1)

One of
[nat.1](a)
or
[nat.1](b)
holds, and one of
\alpha_{\otimes}
or
\alpha_{\oplus}
is an isomorphism.

[nat.1]

\textstyle{\top\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\top}}
\scriptstyle{m_{\top}}
\textstyle{G(\top)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\oplus}}
\scriptstyle{\tiny{(a)}}
\textstyle{F(\top)}

or

\textstyle{F(\bot)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{n_{\bot}}
\textstyle{G(\bot)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\bot}}
\scriptstyle{\tiny{(b)}}
\textstyle{\bot}

(2)

One of
[nat.1](a)
or
[nat.1](b)
holds and one of

[nat.2]

\textstyle{G(A)\otimes F(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\alpha_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\oplus}\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\tiny{(a)}}
\textstyle{G(A)\otimes G(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}^{G}}
\textstyle{F(A)\otimes F(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}^{F}}
\textstyle{F(A\otimes B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{G(A\otimes B)}

or

\textstyle{F(A)\otimes G(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\otimes}\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\alpha_{\oplus}}
\scriptstyle{\tiny{(b)}}
\textstyle{G(A)\otimes G(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}^{G}}
\textstyle{F(A)\otimes F(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}^{F}}
\textstyle{F(A\otimes B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{G(A\otimes B)}

or

\textstyle{G(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}^{G}}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\oplus}}
\scriptstyle{\tiny{(c)}}
\textstyle{G(A)\oplus G(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\alpha_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}^{F}}
\textstyle{F(A)\oplus F(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\otimes}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{G(A)\oplus F(B)}

or

\textstyle{G(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}^{G}}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\oplus}}
\scriptstyle{\tiny{(d)}}
\textstyle{G(A)\oplus G(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\oplus}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F(A)\oplus F(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\alpha_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(A)\oplus G(B)}

holds.

(3)

\alpha_{\otimes}^{-1}=\alpha_{\oplus}

(4)

\alpha^{\prime}:=(\alpha_{\oplus},\alpha_{\otimes}):G\Rightarrow F
is a linear transformation.

for example gives

Recall that a linear functor is
normal
in case both
m_{\top}
and
n_{\bot}
are isomorphisms. We observe:

Lemma 11
.

For a mix Frobenius functor,
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
, between isomix categories the following are equivalent:

(1)

n_{\bot}:F(\bot)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot
or
m_{\top}:\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F(\top)
is an isomorphism;

(2)

F
is a normal functor;

(3)

F
is an isomix functor.

Proof 3.5
.

(i)
\Rightarrow
(ii):

Note that, as
F
is a mix functor
F({\sf m})=n_{\bot}{\sf m}~m_{\top}
. As the mix map
{\sf m}
is an isomorphism so is
F({\sf m})
which implies that if
n_{\bot}
is an isomorphism then
m_{\top}
must be an isomorphism and vice versa. Thus,
F
will be a normal functor.

(ii)
\Rightarrow
(iii):

If
F
is normal then
n_{\bot}
and
m_{\top}
are isomorphisms and so

m_{\top}F({\sf m}^{-1})n_{\bot}={\sf m}^{-1}F({\sf m}^{-1})=m_{\top}^{-1}{\sf m}^{-1}n_{\bot}^{-1}F({\sf m})=n_{\bot}{\sf m}~m_{\top}

(iii)
\Rightarrow
(i):

The mix-preservation for
F
makes
n_{\bot}
a section (and
m_{\top}
a retraction) while the isomix-preservation makes
m_{\bot}
a retraction (and
m_{\top}
a section).
This means
n_{\bot}
is an isomorphism (
m_{\top}
is an isomorphism).

Corollary 12
.

\alpha:=(\alpha_{\otimes},\alpha_{\oplus})
is a linear natural isomorphism between isomix Frobenius linear functors if and only if
\alpha_{\otimes}=\alpha_{\oplus}^{-1}
.

Proof 3.6
.

Note that if we can establish
[nat.1](a)
or
(b)
then we can prove that
\alpha_{\otimes}\alpha_{\oplus}=1
and, as
\alpha_{\otimes}
is an isomorphism it follows that
\alpha_{\oplus}\alpha_{\otimes}=1
.
Thus, it suffices to show that
[nat.1](a)
holds:

m_{\top}\alpha_{\oplus}G({\sf m}^{-1})n_{\bot}=m_{\top}F({\sf m}^{-1})\alpha_{\oplus}n_{\bot}=m_{\top}F({\sf m}^{-1})n_{\bot}={\sf m}^{-1}=m_{\top}G({\sf m}^{-1})n_{\bot}

However, as
G({\sf m}^{-1})n_{\bot}
is an isomorphism, it follows that
m_{\top}\alpha_{\oplus}=m_{\top}
.

Lemma
10
and Corollary
12
are generalizations of
[
DP08
, Proposition 7]
.
[
DP08
, Proposition 7]
states the following:

Let
\mathbb{X}
and
\mathbb{Y}
be monoidal categories and
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv B\in\mathbb{X}
. If
F,G:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
are Frobenius monoidal functors with a natural transformation
\alpha:F\Rightarrow G
which is both monoidal and comonoidal, then
\alpha_{A}
is invertible.

For these special linear isomorphisms with
\alpha_{\otimes}=\alpha_{\oplus}^{-1}
we can simplify the coherence requirements:

Lemma 13
.

Suppose
F
and
G
are Frobenius functors and
\alpha:F\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G
is a natural isomorphism then:

(1)

If
\alpha:F\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G
is
\otimes
-monoidal and
\oplus
-comonoidal then
(\alpha,\alpha^{-1})
is a linear transformation;

(2)

If
F
and
G
are strong Frobenius functors and
\alpha
is
\otimes
-monoidal and
\oplus
-monoidal then
(\alpha,\alpha^{-1})
is a linear transformation.

Proof 3.7
.

(1)

If
\alpha
is
\otimes
-monoidal and
\oplus
-comonoidal then so is
\alpha^{-1}
supporting the possibility that it is a component of a linear transformation.
Considering
[LT.1]
we show that
(\alpha,\alpha^{-1})
satisfies this requirement as:

\textstyle{F(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}=\nu^{R}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{G(A\oplus B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{n_{\oplus}=\nu^{R}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(A)\oplus F(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\alpha\oplus\alpha}
\textstyle{G(A)\oplus G(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha^{-1}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{F(A)\oplus G(B)}

The remaining requirements follow in a similar manner.

(2)

When the laxors for the functors are isomorphisms then being monoidal implies being comonoidal.

3.2.
Dagger mix categories

Conventionally, in categorical quantum mechanics a dagger is defined as a contravariant functor which is an involution that is stationary on objects
(A^{\dagger}=A)
. Before proceeding to define the dagger functor for LDCs, the notion of the opposite LDC and whence the notion of a contravariant linear functors have to be developed. For LDCs we cannot expect the dagger to be stationary on objects, however, it is still possible that it can act like an involution.

If
(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)
is a linear distributive category, the
opposite linear distributive category
is
(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)^{\mathsf{op}}:=(\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}},\oplus,\bot,\otimes,\top)
where
\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}
is the usual opposite category with the monoidal structures are flipped as follows:

\otimes^{\mathsf{op}}:=\oplus~~~~~~~\top^{\mathsf{op}}:=\bot~~~~~~~\oplus^{\mathsf{op}}:=\otimes~~~~~~~\bot^{\mathsf{op}}:=\top

(\_)^{\mathsf{op}}
is an endo functor for the category of LDCs and linear functors. It is an involution:

(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)^{{\mathsf{op}}~{\mathsf{op}}}=(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)
.

Let
(F_{\otimes},F_{\oplus}):(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)
be a linear functor. The opposite linear functor
(F_{\otimes},F_{\oplus})^{\mathsf{op}}:(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)^{\mathsf{op}}
given by the pair of opposite functors
(F_{\oplus}^{\mathsf{op}},F_{\otimes}^{\mathsf{op}})
. Observe that
F^{\mathsf{op}}
is a mix Frobenius linear functor if and only if
F
is.

{defi}

A
dagger linearly distributive category
(
\dagger
-LDC), is an LDC,
\mathbb{X}
, with a contravariant Frobenius linear functor
(\_)^{\dagger}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
which is a linear involutive equivalence
(\_)^{\dagger}~\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv~(\_)^{\dagger^{\mathsf{op}}}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
.

First note that saying this is an
involutive
equivalence asserts that the unit and counit of the equivalence are the same (although one is in the opposite category). Thus, the adjunction expands to take the form
(\imath,\imath):(\_)^{\dagger}~\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv~(\_)^{\dagger^{\mathsf{op}}}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
. However, the unit and counit are linear natural transformations so
\imath
expands to
\imath=(\imath_{\otimes},\imath_{\oplus})
. As the dagger functor is
a left adjoint, it is strong and, thus, is normal. Furthermore, as the unit of an equivalence,
\imath
is a linear natural isomorphism. This means
\imath=(\imath_{\otimes},\imath_{\oplus})
satisfies the requirements of Lemma
10
, implying that
\imath_{\otimes}^{-1}=\imath_{\oplus}
. Simplifying notation we shall set
\iota:=\imath_{\oplus}
so the unit linear transformation is
\imath:=(\iota^{-1},\iota)
. We then can simplify the requirements of
\imath
to the map

\iota:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}
which we refer to as the
involutor
.

A
symmetric
\dagger
-LDC
is a
\dagger
-LDC which is a symmetric LDC for which the dagger is a symmetric linear functor. A
cyclic
\dagger
-
*
-autonomous category
is a

\dagger
-LDC with chosen left are right duals and a cyclor which is preserved by the dagger. A
\dagger
-
mix
category is a
\dagger
-LDC for which
(\_)^{\dagger}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}

is a mix functor. As the dagger functor is strong (and so normal) if the category is an isomix category then being
\dagger
-mix
already implies that
the dagger is an isomix functor. Thus, a
\dagger
-isomix
category is a
\dagger
-mix category which happens to be an isomix category.

In the remainder of the section, we unfold the definition of a
\dagger
-isomix category and give the coherence requirements explicitly.

Proposition 14
.

A dagger linearly distributive category is an LDC with a functor
(\_)^{\dagger}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
and

\displaystyle\text{ \bf involutor: }A

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\iota}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}

]

and two symmetric diagrams for

\iota_{A^{\dagger}}=(\iota_{A}^{-1})^{\dagger}:A^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger\dagger\dagger}

The structure is presented using strong monoidal laxors: to form a linear functor the laxor
\lambda_{\oplus}
needs to be reversed by taking its inverse. Then, we have
\nu_{\otimes}^{l}=\nu_{\otimes}^{r}:=\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1}
and
\nu_{\oplus}^{l}=\nu_{\oplus}^{r}:=\lambda_{\otimes}
. Once this adjustment is made all the required coherences for
\dagger
to be a linear functor are present.

.

The coherences for the involutor asserts that it is a monoidal transformation for both the tensor and par: by Lemma

(ii) this suffices to show that it is a linear transformation.

It is important to note that one may not have a legal proof net inside a
\dagger
-box. This complicates the correctness criterion. However, the required correctness criterion is discussed in
[
MP05
]
.

3.4.
Functors for
\dagger
-linearly distributive categories

Clearly the functors and transformations between
\dagger
-LDCs must “preserve” the dagger in some sense. Precisely we have:

{defi}

F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
is a
\dagger
-linear functor
between
\dagger
-LDCs when
F
is a linear functor equipped with a linear natural isomorphism

\rho^{F}=(\rho_{\otimes}^{F}:F_{\otimes}(A^{\dagger})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A)^{\dagger},\rho_{\oplus}^{F}:F_{\otimes}(A)^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A^{\dagger}))
called the
preservator
,
such that the following diagrams commute:

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(\iota)}
[
\dagger
-LF.1]
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X)^{\dagger\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\rho^{F}_{\oplus})^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\scriptstyle{F_{\oplus}(\iota)}
[
\dagger
-LF.2]
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X)^{\dagger\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\rho^{F}_{\otimes})^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

In case that
F
is a normal mix functor between
\dagger
-isomix categories, then by Lemma
11
,
F
is an isomix functor and, therefore by Corollary
12
, the preservators become inverses,
\rho^{F}_{\otimes}=(\rho^{F}_{\oplus})^{-1}
.
This means the squares
[
\dagger
-LF.1]
and
[
\dagger
-LF.2]
coincide to give a single condition for the tensor preservator:

\textstyle{F(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\scriptstyle{F(\iota)}
[
\dagger
-isomix]
\textstyle{F(X)^{\dagger\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\rho^{F}_{\otimes})^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{F(X^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(X^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

In case when
F
is an isomix functor, by Lemma
10
,
\rho:=\rho_{\otimes}
is monoidal on
\otimes
and comonoidal on
\oplus
:
