For linear natural transformations
(\beta_{\otimes},\beta_{\oplus}):F\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G
between
\dagger
-linear functors, we demand that
\beta_{\otimes}
and
\beta_{\oplus}
are related by:

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A^{\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{\beta_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{G_{\otimes}(A^{\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{G}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{(F_{\oplus}(X))^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\beta_{\oplus}^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{(G_{\oplus}(X))^{\dagger}}

\textstyle{(G_{\otimes}(X))^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{G}_{\oplus}}
\scriptstyle{\beta_{\otimes}^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{(F_{\otimes}(X))^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{G_{\oplus}(A^{\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\beta_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A^{\dagger})}

Notice that this means that
\beta_{\otimes}
is completely determined by
\beta_{\oplus}
in the following sense:

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(\iota)}
\scriptstyle{\beta_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{G_{\otimes}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{G_{\otimes}(\iota)}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{\beta_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{G_{\otimes}(A^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{G}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\beta_{\oplus}^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{G_{\oplus}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

Because the vertical maps are isomorphisms, this diagram can be used to express
\beta_{\otimes}
in terms of
\beta_{\oplus}
. Similarly,
\beta_{\oplus}
can be expressed in terms
of
\beta_{\otimes}
. Thus, it is possible to express the coherences in terms of just one of these transformations.

3.5.
Examples of
\dagger
-LDCs

In this section, we discuss some basic examples of
\dagger
-isomix categories. The first example is a compact LDC. The example of Finiteness spaces is non-compact and all these examples are
*
-autonomous category. These categories all have a non-stationary dagger functor. More examples of
\dagger
-isomix categories can be found in Section
5.6
.

3.5.1.
Finite dimensional framed vector spaces

In this section we describe the category of “framed” finite dimensional vector spaces, where a frame in this context is just a
choice of basis. Thus, the objects in this category are vector spaces with a chosen basis while the maps, ignoring the basis, are simply homomorphisms of
the vector spaces.

The category of finite dimensional framed vectors spaces,
{\sf FFVec}_{K}
, is a monoidal category defined as follows:

Objects:

The objects are pairs
(V,{\cal V})
where
V
is a finite dimensional
K
-vector space and
{\cal V}=\{v_{1},...,v_{n}\}
is a basis.

Maps:

A map
(V,{\cal V})\xrightarrow{f}(W,{\cal W})
is a linear map
V\xrightarrow{f}W
in
{\sf FdVec}_{K}
.

Tensor:

(V,{\cal V})\otimes(W,{\cal W})=(V\otimes W,\{v\otimes w|v\in{\cal V},w\in{\cal W}\})
where
V\otimes W
is the usual tensor product. The unit is

(K,\{e\})
where
e
is the unit of the field
K
.

To define the “dagger” we must first choose a conjugation
\overline{(\_)}:K\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}K
(see more details in Section
4.2
), that is a field homomorphism with
k=\overline{(\overline{k})}
. The
canonical example being conjugation of the complex numbers, however, the conjugation can be arbitrarily chosen – so could also, for example, be the identity.
This conjugation then can be extended to a (covariant) functor:

\overline{(\_)}:{\sf FFVec}_{K}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf FFVec}_{K};\begin{array}[c]{c}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 17.80003pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr\cr\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-14.53615pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{(V,{\cal V})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-16.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.75pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{f}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-24.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern-17.80003pt\raise-32.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{(W,{\cal W})}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\end{array}\mapsto\begin{array}[c]{c}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 5.5pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr\cr\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-5.5pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\overline{(V,{\cal V})}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-15.08888pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-2.83888pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\overline{f}}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-24.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern-5.5pt\raise-30.17776pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\overline{(W,{\cal W})}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\end{array}

where
\overline{(V,{\cal V})}
is the vector space with the same basis but with the conjugate action
c~\overline{\cdot}~v=\overline{c}\cdot v
. The conjugate
homomorphism,
\overline{f}
, is then the same underlying map which is homomorphism between the conjugate spaces.

{\sf FFVec}_{K}
is also a compact closed category with
(V,{\cal B})^{*}=(V^{*},\{\widetilde{b_{i}}|b_{i}\in{\cal B}\})
where

V^{*}=V\multimap K~~~~\mbox{and}~~~~\widetilde{b_{i}}:V\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}K;\left(\sum_{j}\beta_{j}\cdot b_{j}\right)\mapsto\beta_{i}

This makes
(\_)^{*}:{\sf FFVec}_{K}^{\rm op}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf FFVec}_{K}
a contravariant functor whose action is determined by precomposition. Finally, we
define the “dagger” to be the composite
(V,{\cal B})^{\dagger}=\overline{(V,{\cal B})^{*}}
.

This is a compact LDC with tensor and par being identified (so the linear distribution is the associator) and is isomix. We must show that it is a
\dagger
-LDC.
Towards this aim we define the required natural transformations on the basis:

\lambda_{\otimes}=\lambda_{\oplus}:(V,{\cal V})^{\dagger}\otimes(W,{\cal W})^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}((V,{\cal V})\otimes(W,{\cal W}))^{\dagger};\widetilde{v_{i}}\otimes\widetilde{w_{j}}\mapsto\widetilde{v_{i}\otimes w_{j}}

\lambda_{\top}=\lambda_{\bot}:(K,\{e\})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(K,\{e\})^{\dagger};k\mapsto\overline{k}

\iota:(V,{\cal V})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}((V,{\cal V})^{\dagger})^{\dagger};v\mapsto\lambda f.f(v)

Note that the last transformation is given in a basis independent manner. Importantly, it may also be given in a basis dependent manner as

\iota(v_{i})=\widetilde{\widetilde{v_{i}}}
as the behaviour of these two maps is the same when applied to the basis of
(V,{\cal V})^{\dagger}
namely
the elements
\widetilde{v_{j}}
:

\iota(v_{i})(\widetilde{v_{j}})=(\lambda f.f(v_{i}))\widetilde{v_{j}}=\widetilde{v_{j}}v_{i}=\partial_{i,j}=\widetilde{\widetilde{v_{i}}}(\widetilde{v_{j}})

Also note that
\widetilde{v_{i}\otimes w_{j}}=(\widetilde{v_{i}}\otimes\widetilde{w_{j}})u_{\otimes}
, where
u_{\otimes}:K\otimes K\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}K
is the multiplication of the field.
With these definitions in hand it is straightforward to check that this gives a
\dagger
-LDC by checking the required coherences on basis elements.
To demonstrate the technique consider the coherence
[
\dagger
-ldc.4]
:

\textstyle{A\oplus B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota\oplus\iota}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\textstyle{((A\oplus B)^{\dagger})^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\otimes}^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}\oplus(B^{\dagger})^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{(A^{\dagger}\otimes B^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

We must show (identifying tensor and par) that
\lambda_{\otimes}^{\dagger}(\iota(a_{i}\otimes b_{j}))=\lambda_{\otimes}(\iota\otimes\iota(a_{i}\otimes b_{j}))
. Now the result is a
higher-order term so it suffices to show the evaluations on basis elements are the same. This means we need to show:

\lambda_{\otimes}^{\dagger}(\iota(a_{i}\otimes b_{j}))(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})=\lambda_{\otimes}(\iota\otimes\iota(a_{i}\otimes b_{j}))(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})

\displaystyle(\lambda_{\otimes}(\iota\otimes\iota(a_{i}\otimes b_{j})))(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\lambda_{\otimes}(\widetilde{\widetilde{a_{i}}}\otimes\widetilde{\widetilde{b_{j}}}))(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\widetilde{\widetilde{a_{i}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{j}}})(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})(\widetilde{\widetilde{a_{i}}}\otimes\widetilde{\widetilde{b_{j}}})u_{\otimes}~~~\mbox{(diagrammatic order)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\partial_{p,i}\partial_{q,j}

\displaystyle(\lambda_{\otimes}^{\dagger}(\iota(a_{i}\otimes b_{j})))(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\lambda_{\otimes}^{\dagger}(\widetilde{\widetilde{a_{i}\otimes b_{j}}}))(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\widetilde{a_{p}}\otimes\widetilde{b_{q}})\lambda_{\otimes}\widetilde{\widetilde{a_{i}\otimes b_{j}}}~~~\mbox{(diagrammatic order)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\widetilde{a_{p}\otimes b_{q}}\widetilde{\widetilde{a_{i}\otimes b_{j}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\partial_{p,i}\partial_{q,j}

Thus,
{\sf FFVec}_{K}
is a compact
\dagger
-isomix category where the
\dagger
functor shifts objects i.e.,
A\neq A^{\dagger}
.

3.5.2.
Finiteness matrices

Finiteness spaces were introduced by Ehrhard,
[
Ehr05
]
, as a model of linear logic. The type system can be used to produce a typed system for infinite
dimensional matrix multiplication in which no sums become infinite. This system of infinite dimensional matrices forms an isomix
*
-autonomous category.
If these matrices have entries in the complex numbers then there is a natural notion of conjugation and this gives a
\dagger
-isomix category. We shall see that
by taking the core of this category, which is the category of finite dimensional matrices, one obtains a basic example of a
mixed unitary category as described in Section
5
of this paper. This example is also explored further in the sequels to this paper
[
CS19a
,
CS19b
]
.

{defi}

A
finiteness space
is a pair
X:=(|X|,\mathcal{F})
with
|X|
a set, called the
web
, and
\mathcal{F}
be a subset of
\mathcal{P}(|X|)
such that
\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}^{\perp\perp}
where

\mathcal{F}^{\perp}:=\{x^{\prime}\subseteq X|\forall x\in\mathcal{F}.x\cap x^{\prime}\text{ is finite}\}.

The elements of
\mathcal{F}
are called the
finitary sets
of the finiteness space of
X
, and the elements of
\mathcal{F}^{\perp}
are called
cofinitary sets
.

Observe that if the web of
X
is finite, then
\mathcal{F}
is forced to be the whole powerset of
X
. Finiteness spaces organize themselves into a (symmetric)
*
-autonomous category,
{\sf FRel}
:

Objects:

Finiteness spaces
X:=(|X|,\mathcal{F})
.

Maps:

A map
R:(|X|,\mathcal{F})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(|Y|,\mathcal{G})
is a
finiteness relation
that is a relation
R:|X|\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}|Y|
so that:

•:

For all
x\in\mathcal{F}
,
xR\in\mathcal{G}
where
xR=\{y|y\in Y,\text{ there exists }b\in x\text{ such that }bRy\}

•:

For all
y\in\mathcal{G}^{\perp}
,
Ry\in\mathcal{F}^{\perp}
where
Ry=\{x|x\in X,\text{ there exists }t\in y\text{ such that }xRt\}

Composition and identities:

same as in sets and relations.

Tensor:

Given finiteness spaces
X=(|X|,\mathcal{F})
, and
Y=(|Y|,\mathcal{G})
,

X\otimes Y:=(|X|\times|Y|,\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{G})\text{ where}

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{G}

\displaystyle:=~\downarrow\{u\times v|u\in\mathcal{F},v\in\mathcal{G}\}

\displaystyle~=~\{w|\exists u\in\mathcal{F},v\in\mathcal{G}.w\subseteq u\times v\}

This is well-defined as
\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{G})^{\perp\perp}
is proven in
[
Ehr05
]
Lemma 2.

Given maps
R:X_{1}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y_{1}
and
S:X_{2}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y_{2}
:

R\otimes S:=\{((x_{1},x_{2}),(y_{1},y_{2}))|(x_{1},y_{1})\in R,(x_{2},y_{2})\in S\}

Monoidal tensor unit:

\top:=(\{*\},\mathcal{P}(\{*\}))

Dualizing functor:

(X,\mathcal{F})^{*}:=(X,\mathcal{F}^{\perp})

Finiteness spaces with finiteness relations,
{\sf FRel}
, form an isomix
*
-autonomous category, where the objects in the core are precisely the objects whose webs are finite sets.
There is a faithful underlying structure preserving functor
U:{\sf FRel}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf Rel}
.

The category of finiteness matrices over the complex numbers,
{\sf FMat}(\mathbb{C})
, can be built from the category of finiteness spaces:

Objects:

Finiteness spaces
X=(|X|,\mathcal{F})
;

Maps:

M:X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y
, matrices
M:|X|\times|Y|\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C};(x,y)\mapsto M_{x,y}
such that
{\sf supp}(M)=\{(x,y)|M_{x,y}\not=0\}
is a finiteness relation;

Composition:

If
M:X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y
and
N:Y\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Z
then
(MN)_{x,z}=\sum_{y\in Y}M_{x,y}N_{y,z}
where for fixed
x
and
z
both
M_{x,y}
and

N_{y,z}
are non-zero for only finitely many
y
as this is the intersection of a finitary set of
Y
with a cofinitary set of
Y
. Identity maps are given as usual
by diagonal matrices.

Tensor:

If
M:X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y
and
N:X^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y^{\prime}
then
M\otimes N:X\otimes X^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y\otimes Y^{\prime};((x,y),(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}))\mapsto M_{x,y}N_{x^{\prime},y^{\prime}}
;

Dual and dagger:

If
M:X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y
then
M^{*}:Y^{*}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}X^{*};(y,x)\mapsto M_{x,y}
while
M^{\dagger}:Y^{*}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}X^{*};(y,x)\mapsto\overline{M_{x,y}}
.

The coherence maps for the isomix
*
-autonomous of
{\sf FMat}(\mathbb{C})
are simply the characteristic functions of the relations which give the coherence maps in
{\sf FRel}
.
The support gives a colax 2-functor from
{\sf supp}:{\sf FMat}(\mathbb{C})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf FRel}
where
{\sf supp}(MN)\subseteq{\sf supp}(M){\sf supp}(N)
.

3.5.3.
Category of abstract state spaces

This model is inspired by the category of convex operational models
[
BW11
]
.
The following is a way to construct new
\dagger
-isomix categories from an exisiting one.

{defi}

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a
\dagger
-isomix category. Define
\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
as follows:

Objects:

(A,e_{A}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot,u_{A}:\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A)

Arrows:

f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\in\mathbb{X}
such that the following diagram commutes:

\textstyle{\top\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{A}}
\scriptstyle{u_{B}}
\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f}
\scriptstyle{e_{A}}
\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{e_{B}}
\textstyle{\bot}

Identity arrow and composition are inherited directly from
\mathbb{X}
.
\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
is a LDC:

\otimes
on objects:

(A,e_{A},u_{A})\otimes(B,e_{B},u_{B}):=(A\otimes B,e^{\prime},u^{\prime})
where,
e^{\prime}:=\mathsf{mx}(e_{A}\oplus e_{B})u_{\oplus}
and
u^{\prime}:=u_{\otimes}^{-1}(u_{A}\otimes u_{B})
. The unit of
\otimes
is given by
(\top,{\sf m}^{-1}:\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot,1_{\top})
.

\oplus
on objects:

(A,e_{A},u_{A})\oplus(B,e_{B},u_{B}):=(A\oplus B,e^{\prime},u^{\prime})
where,
e^{\prime}:=(e_{A}\oplus e_{B})u_{\oplus}
and
u^{\prime}:=u_{\otimes}^{-1}(u_{A}\otimes u_{B})\mathsf{mx}
. The unit of
\oplus
is
(\bot,1_{\bot},{\sf m}^{-1}:\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot)

\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
is also
\dagger
-isomix category with

(A,e,u)^{\dagger}:=(A^{\dagger},u^{\dagger}\lambda_{\bot}^{-1},\lambda_{\top}e^{\dagger})

All the basic natural isomorphisms are inherited from
\mathbb{X}
. Hence,
\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
is a
\dagger
-isomix category.

4.
Daggers, duals, and conjugation

The goal of this section is to review the interaction of the dualizing, conjugation and dagger functors.
In dagger compact closed categories, the dagger functor
(\_)^{\dagger}
, and the dualizing functor
(\_)^{*}

commute with each other and their composite gives the conjugate functor
(\_)_{*}
. Similary,
(\_)_{*}
and
(\_)^{*}

when composed gives the dagger functor. Our aim is to generalize these interactions to
\dagger
-LDCs and to achieve
this at a reasonable level of abstraction. To achieve this we shall need the notion which we here refer to as “conjugation”
but was investigated by Egger in
[
Egg11
]
under the moniker of “involution” (which clashes with our usage).

4.1.
Duals

The reverse of an LDC,
\mathbb{X}
, written
\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{rev}}:=(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)^{\sf rev}

=(\mathbb{X},\otimes^{\sf rev},\top,\oplus^{\sf rev},\bot)
where,

A\otimes^{\sf rev}B:=B\otimes A~~~~~~~~~~~A\oplus^{\sf rev}B:=B\oplus A

and the associators and distributors are adjusted accordingly. Similar to the opposite of an LDC, we have
(\mathbb{X}^{\sf rev})^{\sf rev}=\mathbb{X}
.

In a
*
-autonomous category, taking the left (or right) linear dual of an object extends to a Frobenius linear functor as follows:

\displaystyle(\_)^{*}:(\mathbb{X}^{\sf op})^{\sf rev}

These maps are op-monoidal and op-comonoidal laxors, hence are isomorphisms, which satisfy the obvious coherences. Thus,
(\_)^{*}
is a strong Frobenius linear functor.

In the rest of the section, we will write
(\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}})^{\mathsf{rev}}
as
\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}\mathsf{rev}}
.

Lemma 19
.

If
\mathbb{X}
is an isomix category, then
(\_)^{*}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}\mathsf{rev}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
is an isomix functor.

Proof 4.1
.

(\_)^{*}
is a strong Frobenius functor, by Lemma
11
, it suffices to prove that
(\_)^{*}
preserves mix, i.e.,
(\_)^{*}
is a mix functor i.e., we need to show that
n_{\bot}\!~{\sf m}~m_{\top}:\top^{*}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot^{*}={\sf m}^{*}

is a linear equivalence of Frobenius linear functors.

Proof 4.2
.

The proof is straightforward in the graphical calculus.

For a cyclic
*
-autonomous category, we can straighten out this equivalence to be a dualizing involutive equivalence (i.e. so that the unit and counit are equal):

Lemma 21
.

(\eta^{\prime},\epsilon^{\prime})::(\_)^{*}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv((\_)^{*})^{\mathsf{op}\mathsf{rev}}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}\mathsf{rev}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
where
\eta^{\prime}_{\otimes}={\eta^{\prime}_{\oplus}}^{-1}:=\eta_{\otimes}\psi^{-1}
,
\epsilon^{\prime}_{\otimes}=\epsilon^{\prime}_{\oplus}:=\epsilon\psi^{*}
and
\eta^{\prime}=\epsilon^{\prime}
.

4.2.
Conjugation

Recall the following structure from Egger
[
Egg11
]
:

{defi}

A
conjugation
for a monoidal category
(X,\otimes,I)
consists of a functor
\overline{(\_)}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{rev}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
with natural isomorphisms:

\overline{A}\otimes\overline{B}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.99652pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\chi$}}}\overline{B\otimes A}~~~~~~~~~~~~~\overline{\overline{A}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.77812pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\varepsilon$}}}A

called respectively the (tensor reversing)
conjugating laxor
and the
conjugator

such that

\overline{\overline{\overline{A}}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to34.6933pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\overline{\varepsilon_{A}}=\varepsilon_{\overline{A}}$}}}\overline{A}

and

\textstyle{(\overline{A}\otimes\overline{B})\otimes\overline{C}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{\chi\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\bf[CF.1]_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{\overline{A}\otimes(\overline{B}\otimes\overline{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\chi}
\textstyle{\overline{(B\otimes A)}\otimes\overline{C}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\chi}
\textstyle{\overline{A}\otimes\overline{(C\otimes B)}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\chi}
\textstyle{\overline{C\otimes(B\otimes A)}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\overline{a_{\otimes}^{-1}}}
\textstyle{\overline{(C\otimes B)\otimes A}}

\textstyle{\overline{\overline{A}}\otimes\overline{\overline{B}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\chi}
\scriptstyle{\varepsilon\otimes\varepsilon}

\textstyle{A\otimes B}

\scriptstyle{\varepsilon}

A monoidal category is
conjugative
when it has a conjugation functor.

A symmetric monoidal category, which is conjugative, is
symmetric conjugative
in case it satisfies the additional coherence:

\textstyle{\overline{A}\otimes\overline{B}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{c_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{\chi}
\scriptstyle{\bf[CF.3]_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{\overline{B\otimes A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\overline{c_{\otimes}}}
\textstyle{\overline{B}\otimes\overline{A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\chi}
\textstyle{\overline{A\otimes B}}

Notice that we have not specified any coherence for the unit
I
. This is because the expected coherences are automatic:

Lemma 22
.

Egg11
, Lemma 2.3]

For every conjugative monoidal category, there exists a unique isomorphism
I\xrightarrow{\chi^{\!\!\!\circ}}\overline{I}
such that

\textstyle{I\otimes\overline{A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\chi^{\!\!\!\circ}\otimes 1}

\textstyle{\overline{A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{\overline{A\otimes I}}

{defi}

[
Egg11

A
conjugative LDC
is a linearly distributive category
(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\oplus,\bot)
together with a conjugating functor
\overline{(\_)}:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
and natural isomorphisms:

\overline{A}\otimes\overline{B}\xrightarrow{\chi_{\otimes}}\overline{B\otimes A}~~~~~~~~~~~~\overline{A\oplus B}\xrightarrow{\chi_{\oplus}}\overline{B}\oplus\overline{A}~~~~~~~~~~~~\overline{\overline{A}}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A

such that
(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\top,\chi_{\otimes},\varepsilon)
and
(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\bot,\chi_{\oplus}^{-1},\varepsilon)
are conjugative (symmetric) monoidal categories with respect to the conjugating functor and the following diagrams commute:

\textstyle{\overline{B\oplus C}\otimes\overline{A}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\chi_{\oplus}\otimes 1}

\textstyle{\overline{A}\otimes\overline{C\oplus B}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\chi_{\otimes}}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\chi_{\oplus}}
\scriptstyle{\bf[CF.8]}

\scriptstyle{\chi_{\otimes}\oplus 1}
\textstyle{\overline{(B\otimes A)}\oplus\overline{C}}

Note, by Lemma
22
, there exists canonical isomorphisms
\top\xrightarrow{\chi^{\!\!\!\circ}_{\top}}\overline{\top}
and
\bot\xrightarrow{\chi^{\!\!\!\circ}_{\bot}}\overline{\bot}
, hence conjugation is a normal functor. However, the conjugation is not necessarily a mix functor when
\mathbb{X}
is a mix category. For
conjugation to be a mix functor, the following extra condition must be satisfied:

Proposition 23
.

A conjugative LDC is precisely a LDC,
\mathbb{X}
, with a Frobenius adjoint
(\epsilon^{-1},\epsilon):\overline{(\_)}\dashv\overline{(\_)}^{\mathsf{rev}}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{rev}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
where
\epsilon:=(\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1})
. Furthermore, if
\mathbb{X}
is an isomix category and conjugation is a mix functor then conjugation is an isomix equivalence.

Proof 4.4
.

It is clear that
\overline{(\_)}
is a strong Frobenius functor so being mix implies isomix. Also,
\varepsilon
is clearly monoidal for tensor and par. The triangle equalities give
\overline{\varepsilon^{-1}}\varepsilon=1:\overline{A}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\overline{A}
thus
\varepsilon=\overline{\varepsilon}
.

Clearly conjugation should flip left duals into right duals:

Lemma 24
.

If
B\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
is a linear dual then
\overline{A}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv\overline{B}
is a linear dual.

Proof 4.5
.

Suppose
(\eta,\varepsilon):B\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv A
. Then,
(\chi^{\!\!\!\circ}_{\top}\overline{\eta}\chi_{\oplus},\chi_{\otimes}\overline{\varepsilon}\chi^{\!\!\!\circ}_{\bot}):\overline{A}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv\overline{B}
.

When a
*
-autonomous category is cyclic one expects that conjugation should interact with the cyclor in a coherent fashion:

{defi}

[
EM12
]

A
conjugative cyclic
*
-autonomous category
is a conjugative
*
-autonomous category together with a cyclor
A^{*}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.29169pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\psi$}}}\!\!~^{*}\!A
such that

Specifically we have:

Theorem 26
.

Every cyclic,
\dagger
-
*
-autonomous category is a conjugative
*
-autonomous category.

Proof 4.7
.

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a cyclic,
\dagger
-
*
-autonomous category. Then composing adjoints gives the equivalence
(\_)^{\dagger^{*}}\dashv(\_)^{*^{\dagger}}
. To build a conjugation, however,
we need an equivalence between the same functors: to obtain such an equivalence we use the natural equivalence
\omega:(\_)^{\dagger*}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\_)^{*\dagger}
from the cyclor preserving condition for Frobenius linear functors. A conjugative equivalence, in addition, requires that the unit and counit of the equivalence be inverses of each other.
The unit and counit of the equivalence are given by (a) and (b) respectively;

(a)

\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf rev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\mathsf{op}}}}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\eta_{\otimes}^{\prime}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf rev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\mathsf{op}}}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\dagger}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\iota^{-1}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf op}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\dagger^{\mathsf{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\omega}
\scriptstyle{\Longrightarrow}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf oprev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf oprev}}}
\scriptstyle{\dagger^{\mathsf{rev}}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}}

(b)

\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{rev}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\dagger^{\mathsf{rev}}}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\mathsf{rev}}}}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf op}}}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\epsilon^{\prime}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf oprev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf oprev}}}

(a)
and

Next, we show that a conjugation functor together with a dualizing functors gives a
\dagger
:

Theorem 27
.

Every cyclic, conjugative
*
-autonomous category is also a
\dagger
-
*
-autonomous category.

Proof 4.8
.

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a cyclic, conjugative
*
-autonomous category then
\overline{(\_)^{*}}\dashv\overline{(\_)}^{*}
is an equivalence. To build a dagger we need an equivalence on the same
functor: we obtain this by using the natural equivalence
\sigma:\overline{(\_)^{*}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\overline{(\_)}^{*}
from Definition
4.2
. An involutive equivalence, in addition,
requires the unit and counit of the (contravariant) equivalence to be the same map (which we called the involutor,
\iota
). We show that this is the case:

The unit and counit of the equivalence is given by (a) and (b) respectively;

(a)

\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf rev}}}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\eta_{\otimes}^{\prime}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf op}}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf rev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\overline{(\_)}}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\varepsilon^{-1}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf rev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\overline{(\_)}^{\sf rev}}
\scriptstyle{\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\Longrightarrow}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf oprev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf oprev}}}
\scriptstyle{\overline{(\_)}^{\mathsf{op}}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}}

(b)

\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\overline{(\_)}^{\mathsf{op}}}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\mathsf{op}}}}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf rev}}}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\epsilon^{\prime}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}^{\sf oprev}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\_)^{*^{\sf oprev}}}

Observe that for composition of the dualizing functor and the conjugation functor to yield a dagger, and vice versa, a
*
-autonomous category is required to be cyclic with the cyclor being preserved by the conjugation (see Definition
4.2
) and the dagger (see just before Lemma
18
).

4.4.
Examples

In this section, we cover examples of
\dagger
-isomix categories where the
\dagger
is given by conjugation and the dualizing functor.

4.4.1.
Category of a group with conjugation

{defi}

A
group with conjugation
is a group
(G,.,e)
together with a function
\overline{(\_)}:G\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G
such that, for all
g\in G
,
\overline{\overline{g}}=g
, and for all
g,h\in G
,
\overline{g.h}=\overline{h}\overline{g}
, and
\overline{e}=e
.

Let
(G,.,e)
be a group with conjugation. The discrete category
\mathbb{D}{(G,.,e})
whose objects are the elements of the group is a monoidal category with the tensor product given by
g\otimes h:=g.h
, and the monoidal unit
e
. Moreover,
\mathbb{D}{(G,.,e)}
is a compact closed category where
g^{*}:=g^{-1}
and it has a trivial conjugative cyclor (See Definition
4.2
). Thus,
\mathbb{D}{(G,.,e})
is a compact
\dagger
-isomix-
*
-autonomous category with
g^{\dagger}:=\overline{g^{*}}
gives an example of how the conjugation gives rise to a dagger.

Here are some examples of groups with conjugation and the discrete categories given by them:

•

Suppose we fix the group to be
(\mathbb{C},+,0)
where the objects are complex numbers and the tensor product is addition. The dual and conjugation of complex numbers are given as follows:
(a+ib)^{*}=-a-ib
and
\overline{a+ib}:=a-ib
. Hence,

(a+ib)^{\dagger}:=\overline{(a+ib)^{*}}=\overline{(-a-ib)}=-a+ib

•

Consider the multiplicative group
(\mathbb{C}^{*},.,1)
where the objects are non-zero complex numbers and the tensor product is given by multiplication. The dualizing and the conjugation functors are given as follows:

(a+ib)^{*}=c+id,\text{ where }ac-bd=1\text{ and }ad+bc=0

\overline{a+ib}:=a-ib

(a+ib)^{\dagger}
is given by
\overline{(a+ib)^{*}}
.

•

Suppose the group is fixed to be
\mathbb{D}{(P(x),+,0})
where
P(x)
is a polynomial ring.

\mathbb{D}{(P(x),+,0})
is a conjugative compact closed category:
P(x)^{*}=-P(x)
and
\overline{P(x)}=P(-x)
. Then,
P(x)^{\dagger}=-P(-x)
.

•

Consider the general linear group of degree 2,
(\mathbb{M}_{2},.,I_{2})
over complex numbers. Then, the discrete category
\mathbb{D}(\mathbb{M}_{2},.,I_{2})
has a dualizing functor given by matrix inverse and conjugation is given by conjugate transpose:
\overline{\left(\begin{matrix}a+ib&m+in\\
c+id&p+iq\end{matrix}\right)}:=\left(\begin{matrix}a-ib&c-id\\
m-in&p-iq\end{matrix}\right)
. Then,
\mathbb{D}(\mathbb{M}_{2},.,I_{2})
is a
\dagger
-isomix
*
-autonomous category with:

\left(\begin{matrix}a+ib&m+in\\
c+id&p+iq\end{matrix}\right)^{\dagger}:=\overline{\left(\begin{matrix}a+ib&m+in\\
c+id&p+iq\end{matrix}\right)^{*}}=\left(\begin{matrix}a-ib&c-id\\
m-in&p-iq\end{matrix}\right)^{-1}

4.4.2.
Chu Spaces

Applications of Chu Spaces to represent quantum systems have been studied in
[
Abr12
]
,
[
Abr13
]
.
In this section we show that the Chu construction over a closed conjugative monoidal category,
which has pullbacks, produces a
\dagger
-isomix LDC,
{\sf Chu}_{\mathbb{X}}(I)
. To get
the
*
-autonomous category and
\dagger
-structure on
{\sf Chu}_{\mathbb{X}}(I)
we shall start
by explaining how one can produce conjugative structure on the
{\sf Chu}
category.
To achieve this we iteratively develop the structure of this category, starting with a
conjugative closed monoidal category,
\mathbb{X}
, which is not necessarily symmetric.
Note that the fact that it is conjugative means that it is both left and right closed which
allows us to consider the non-commutative
{\sf Chu}
construction: in this regard
we shall follow Jürgen Koslowski’s construction
[
Kos06
]
using simplified “Chu-cells” on the
same dualizing object to obtain not a
{*}
-linear bicategory but a cyclic
*
-autonomous category.
Furthermore, we shall choose a dualizing object which is conjugative in order to obtain a conjugative
cyclic
*
-autonomous category.

A conjugative object is an object
D
of
\mathbb{X}
with an isomorphism
d:\overline{D}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}D
such that
\overline{d}d=\varepsilon:D\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\overline{\overline{D}}
.
We can then define
{\sf Chu}_{\mathbb{X}}(D)
as follows:

Objects:

(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})
where
\psi_{0}:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}D
and
\psi_{1}:B\otimes A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}D
in
\mathbb{X}
(these are the simplified Chu cells).

Arrows:

(f,g):(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},\psi_{0}^{\prime},\psi_{1}^{\prime})
where
f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\prime}
and
g:B^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
and the following diagrams commutes:

\textstyle{A\otimes B^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes g}
\scriptstyle{f\otimes 1}
\textstyle{A\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi_{0}}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi^{\prime}_{0}}
\textstyle{D}

\textstyle{B^{\prime}\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{g\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes f}
\textstyle{B\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi_{1}}
\textstyle{B^{\prime}\otimes A^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi^{\prime}_{1}}
\textstyle{D}

Compositon:

(f,g)(f^{\prime},g^{\prime}):=(ff^{\prime},g^{\prime}g)
. Composition is well-defined as:

\textstyle{A\otimes B^{\prime\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{f\otimes 1}
\textstyle{A\otimes B^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes g}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{f^{\prime}\otimes 1}
\textstyle{A\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi_{0}}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi^{\prime}_{0}}
\textstyle{A^{\prime\prime}\otimes B^{\prime\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\psi_{0}^{\prime\prime}}
\textstyle{D}

and similarly for the reverse Chu-maps
\psi_{1}
,
\psi^{\prime}_{1}
and
\psi_{1}^{\prime\prime}
.
The
identity maps
are
(1_{A},1_{B}):(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})
as expected.

Tensor product
\otimes
:

(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})\otimes(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},\psi_{0}^{\prime},\psi_{1}^{\prime}):=(A\otimes A^{\prime},E,\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})
, where
E
is the pullback in the following diagram:

\textstyle{E\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\pi_{0}}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\multimap B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\multimap\tilde{\psi_{1}}}
\textstyle{B^{\prime}\reflectbox{$\multimap$}A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\tilde{\psi_{1}^{\prime}}\reflectbox{$\multimap$}A}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\multimap(D\reflectbox{$\multimap$}A)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to18.25pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\simeq$}}}(A^{\prime}\multimap D)\reflectbox{$\multimap$}A}

with

B\otimes A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.24168pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\psi_{1}$}}}BB\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.55556pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\tilde{\psi_{1}}$}}}D\reflectbox{$\multimap$}A~~~~~~~~~~A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}DB^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.55556pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\tilde{\psi_{1}^{\prime}}$}}}A^{\prime}\multimap D

and,

\gamma_{0}:=(A\otimes A^{\prime})\otimes E\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to33.50441pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$1\otimes\pi_{0}$}}}(A\otimes A^{\prime})\otimes(A^{\prime}\multimap B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.64874pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$a_{\otimes}$}}}A\otimes(A^{\prime}\otimes A^{\prime}\multimap B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to46.77496pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$1\otimes eval_{\multimap}$}}}A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.24168pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\psi_{0}^{\prime}$}}}D

\gamma_{1}:=E\otimes(A\otimes A^{\prime})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to31.68343pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\pi_{1}\otimes 1$}}}(B^{\prime}\reflectbox{$\multimap$}A)\otimes(A\otimes A^{\prime})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.92096pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$a_{\otimes}^{-1}$}}}(B^{\prime}\reflectbox{$\multimap$}A\otimes A)\otimes A^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to44.95398pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$eval_{\reflectbox{$\multimap$}}\otimes 1$}}}B^{\prime}\otimes A^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.24168pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\psi_{1}^{\prime}$}}}D

The tensor unit is
(I,D,u_{\otimes}^{l},u_{\otimes}^{r})
.

It is standard that
{\sf Chu}_{\mathbb{X}}(D)
is a (non-commutative)
*
-autonomous category. Furthermore, it is cyclic because

~{}^{*}(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})=(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})^{*}=(B,A,\psi_{1},\psi_{0}).

In addition,
{\sf Chu}_{\mathbb{X}}(D)
is conjugative with

\overline{(A,B,\psi_{0},\psi_{1})}:=(\overline{A},\overline{B},\chi\overline{\psi_{1}}d,\chi\overline{\psi_{0}}d)

and
\overline{(f,g)}=(\overline{f},\overline{g})
.
Finally, being conjugative cyclic
*
-autonomous implies that one has a dagger!

In the case that
\mathbb{X}
is a symmetric monoidal closed category we may recapture the usual Chu construction
[
Bar06
]
, which we denote
{\sf Chus}_{\mathbb{X}}(D)
. Consider the full subcategory
of Chu-objects with special Chu-cells of the form
(A,B,\psi,c_{\otimes}\psi)
in which the symmetry map is used to obtain the second cell, this gives an inclusion

{\sf Chus}_{\mathbb{X}}(D)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf Chu}_{\mathbb{X}}(D)
.

We observe that
\mathbb{X}
is symmetric conjugative when this subcategory is closed to the conjugation:

Lemma 28
.

If
\mathbb{X}
is a conjugative symmetric monoidal closed category and
d:\overline{D}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}D
is an involutive object, then
{\sf Chus}_{\mathbb{X}}(D)
is a conjugative symmetric
*
-autonomous category.

Proof 4.9
.

It suffices to observe that the Chu-cells of
\overline{(A,B,\psi,c_{\otimes}\psi)}
have the right form. Using the coherence of the
involution with symmetry, the first Chu-cell of this object has
\chi\overline{c_{\otimes}\psi}d=c_{\otimes}\chi\overline{\psi}d

which is exactly the symmetry map applied to the second Chu-cell of the object as desired.

To obtain an isomix category one can choose D = I.
{\sf Chus}_{\mathbb{X}}(I)
is an isomix category because the unit for tensor and par are the same (namely
\top=\bot=(I,I,u_{\otimes}^{l}=u_{\otimes}^{r})
). The tensor unit is always a conjugative object since
(\chi^{\!\!\!\circ})^{-1}:\overline{I}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}I
; therefore, this is immediately a conjugative symmetric
*
-autonomous category. Composing the conjugation with the dualizing functor gives us a dagger.

4.4.3.
Category of Hopf Modules of a
*
-autonomous category

In the previous example, starting from a conjugative closed monoidal category with pullbacks, we built a
\dagger
-
*
-autonomous category using the Chu construction. In this example
3
3

3

We thank J-S. P. Lemay for bringing our attention to this example.
, we start with any symmetric
*
-autonomous category,
\mathbb{X}
, and build the category of modules over a Hopf Algebra which is in turn a
\dagger
-
*
-autonomous category.

First of all, it has been already proven in
[
PS09
]
, that the category of Hopf modules over a
\otimes
-Hopf algebra in any symmetric
*
-autonomous category is also a
*
-autonomous category. Then we note that, whenever the Hopf Algebra is cocommutative, the resulting
*
-autonomous category has a conjugation functor. One can construct the dagger functor by composing the conjugation functor and dualizing functor as in Theorem
27
. We establish some basic definitions before describing the category of modules over a Hopf Algerba,
{\mbox{\bf H-Mod}}_{\mathbb{X}}
.

{defi}

A
bialgebra
in a symmetric monoidal category is a 4-tuple

(\nabla:B\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B,e:I\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B,\Delta:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\otimes B,u:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}I)

such that
(A,\nabla,e)
is a monoid and
(A,\Delta,u)
is a comonoid and
\nabla
and
e
are coalgebra homomorphisms with respect to the comultiplication and the counit.

Note that instead of requiring that
\nabla
and
e
are coalgebra homomorphisms, one could equivalently require
\Delta
and
u
are algebra homomorphims with respect to the multiplication and the unit.

A
Hopf algebra
is a bialgebra with an antipode. An
involutive Hopf algebra
is a hopf algebra where the antipode is self-inverse.

A standard example of a Hopf algebra is a group algebra over a field: for all group elements
g
,
\nabla:g\mapsto g\otimes g
,

Lemma 29
.

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
is a symmetric monoidal category, then:

(1)

[
Blu96
, Theroem 3.5]
If
H
is a commutative or a cocommutative Hopf Algebra in
\mathbb{X}
, then
s^{2}=1
where
s
is the antipode:
so it is an involutive Hopf algebra.

(2)

[
Lem19
, Lemma 2.11]
If
H
is a commutative Hopf Algebra, then
s
is a monoid homomorphism. If
H
is a cocommutative
Hopf Algebra, then
s
is a comonoid homomorphism.

{defi}

(B,\nabla,u,\Delta,e)

(M,a_{M}^{l}:B\otimes M\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}M)

\textstyle{M\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{\top\otimes M\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{M}

{defi}

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a
*
-autonomous category and
H
be a Hopf
\otimes
-algebra in
\mathbb{X}
. The category of left H-modules in
\mathbb{X}
,
{\mbox{\bf H-Mod}}_{\mathbb{X}}
has:

Objects:

Left
H
-modules
(A,a_{A}^{l}:H\otimes A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A)
:

Arrows:

A module homomorphism
(A,a_{A}^{L}:H\otimes A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.68407pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f$}}}(B,a_{B}^{L}:H\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B)
is a map
A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.68407pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f$}}}B
such that the following diagram commutes:

\textstyle{H\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{A}^{L}}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes f}
\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f}
\textstyle{H\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{B}^{L}}
\textstyle{B}

[

Futhermore, we can show that the category of Hopf modules is conjugative.

Lemma 30
.

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a symmetric
*
-autonomous category.
{\mbox{\bf H-Mod}}_{\mathbb{X}}
, the category of modules over a cocommutative Hopf Algebra H is a conjugative symmetric
*
-autonomous category.

Thus, one can generate a
\dagger
-isomix category from a symmetric isomix
*
-autonomous category by choosing the Hopf modules over any cocommutative
\otimes

5.
Unitary structure and mixed unitary categories

The objective of this section is to introduce mixed unitary categories (MUCs) and their morphisms. A mixed unitary category consists of
a
unitary category
,
\mathbb{U}
, with a
\dagger
-isomix Frobenius functor
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
into a “large”
\dagger
isomix category
\mathbb{C}
.
We refer to
\mathbb{U}
as the
unitary core
of the MUC. The unitary core is to be regarded as providing the analogue of scalars for the larger
category much as a field provides scalars for an algebra over that field.

The section starts by describing the general notion of unitary structure in a
\dagger
-isomix category. This allows the definition of a unitary category as
a compact
\dagger
-isomix category in which all objects have unitary structure satisfying certain coherence conditions. We then show how to extract
a unitary category from any compact
\dagger
-isomix category using
pre-unitary objects
. This is a useful construction in practice. However, it can
just deliver a trivial unitary category – trivial in the sense that all objects are isomorphic to the units. This means that, in applying the construction, it is
important to identify non-trivial pre-unitary objects to ensure that one is getting something worthwhile out.

Next we show, using the isomix functors
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}
(or
{\sf Mx}_{\downarrow}
) that unitary categories are
\dagger
-linearly equivalent to

\dagger
-monoidal categories and, furthermore, that closed unitary categories are equivalent to
\dagger
-compact closed categories. This provides an
explicit connection from MUCs to the standard notions from categorical quantum mechanics. One contribution of this more general perspective is that through the
constructions in this section one can obtain examples not only of mixed unitary categories but also of
\dagger
-monoidal and
\dagger
-compact closed
categories which might otherwise have been difficult to realize.

The final subsection introduces mixed unitary categories (MUCs). These form the basis for our approach to infinite dimensional categorical quantum mechanics.
A MUC has a unitary core which is a model of classical categorical quantum mechanics extended by a larger setting in which infinite dimensional objects can
be modelled.

5.1.
Unitary structure

The notion of unitary maps is central to both quantum information theory as well as quantum mechanics since the evolution of a closed quantum system is described by such maps. Categorically, within a
\dagger
-category, a unitary map is an isomorphism
f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
such that
f^{-1}=f^{\dagger}
. This definition of unitary isomorphism cannot be used directly within the framework of
\dagger
-LDCs since the types of
f^{-1}:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
and
f^{\dagger}:B^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
are different. It is therefore
apparent that one can only ask to have unitary isomorphisms between certain objects, which we call “unitary objects”:

{defi}

A
\dagger
-isomix category,
\mathbb{X}
has
unitary structure
in case there is an essentially small class of objects
\mathcal{U}
, called the
unitary objects
of
\mathbb{X}
such that

]

(1)

for all
A\in\mathcal{U}
,
A\in\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
, and
A
is equipped with an isomorphism,
\varphi_{A}:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
, called the
unitary structure map
of
A

(2)

\mathcal{U}
is closed to
(\_)^{\dagger}
so that for all
A\in\mathcal{U}
,
\varphi_{A^{\dagger}}=((\varphi_{A})^{-1})^{\dagger}

(3)

for all
A\in\mathcal{U}
, the following diagram commutes:

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A^{\dagger}}}
\textstyle{(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

(4)

\bot,\top\in\mathcal{U}
such that:

\textstyle{\bot\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{\bot}}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\bot}}
\scriptstyle{{\sf m}}
\textstyle{\bot^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\top}^{-1}}
\textstyle{\top^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{\top}^{-1}}
\textstyle{\top}

(5)

If
A,B\in\mathcal{U}
, then
A\otimes B
and
A\oplus B\in\mathcal{U}
such that :

Lemma 33
.

When
A
and
B
is a unitary object in a
\dagger
-isomix category then,
\varphi_{A^{\dagger\dagger}}=(\varphi_{A})^{\dagger\dagger}:A^{\dagger\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger\dagger\dagger}
.

Proof 5.1
.

\varphi_{(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}=((\varphi_{A^{\dagger}})^{-1})^{\dagger}=((((\varphi_{A})^{-1})^{\dagger})^{-1})^{\dagger}=((((\varphi_{A})^{-1})^{-1})^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=((\varphi_{A})^{\dagger})^{\dagger}

Often we shall want the unitary objects to have linear adjoints (or duals) but we shall need the analogue of
\dagger
-duals
(\eta^{\dagger}=c_{\otimes}\epsilon
and
\epsilon^{\dagger}=\eta c_{\otimes})
from categorical quantum mechanics:

{defi}

A
unitary linear duality

(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}B
between unitary objects
A
and
B

Lemma 34
.

Suppose
(\eta_{1},\epsilon_{1}):V_{1}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}U_{1}
and
(\eta_{2},\epsilon_{2}):V_{2}\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}U_{2}
. Then,
(V_{1}\otimes V_{2})\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}(U_{1}\oplus U_{2})
.

We can now define what it means for an isomorphism to be unitary:

{defi}

Suppose
A
and
B
are unitary objects. An isomorphism
A\xrightarrow{f}B
is said to be a
unitary isomorphism
if the following diagram commutes:

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\scriptstyle{f}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{B}}
\textstyle{B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f^{\dagger}}

Observe that
\varphi
is “twisted” natural for all unitary isomorphisms, thus, unitary isomorphisms compose and contain the identity maps. In a category in which the unitary structure maps are identity morphisms, one recovers the usual notion of unitary isomorphisms.

Our next objective is to show that all the coherence isomorphisms between unitary objects are unitary maps. First a warm up:

Lemma 35
.

In a
\dagger
-isomix category with unitary structure:

(1)

If
f
is a unitary isomorphism, then so is
f^{\dagger}
;

(2)

If
f
and
g
are unitary, then so are
f\otimes g
and
f\oplus g
;

(3)

Unitary isomorphisms are closed under composition.

Proof 5.3
.

(1)

Recall that
\varphi_{A^{\dagger}}=(\varphi_{A}^{-1})^{\dagger}
, then
f^{\dagger}
is unitary because

\textstyle{B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\varphi_{B}^{-1})^{\dagger}=\varphi_{B^{\dagger}}}
\scriptstyle{f^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\varphi_{A}^{-1})^{\dagger}=\varphi_{A^{\dagger}}}
\textstyle{B^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}}
\textstyle{A^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f^{{\dagger}{\dagger}}}

is just the dagger functor applied to the unitary diagram of
f
.

(2)

Suppose
f
and
g
are unitary morphisms, then:

\textstyle{A\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A\otimes B}}
\scriptstyle{f\otimes g}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
(nat.
\mathsf{mx}
)

[U.5(b)]
\textstyle{(A\otimes B)^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

(nat.
\lambda_{\oplus})
\textstyle{A\oplus B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}\oplus\varphi_{B}}
\scriptstyle{f\oplus g}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}\oplus B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\oplus B^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A^{\prime}}\otimes\varphi_{B^{\prime}}}

[U.5(b)]
\textstyle{A^{\prime\dagger}\oplus B^{\prime\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\oplus}}

\textstyle{A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
\textstyle{(A^{\prime}\otimes B^{\prime})^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(f\otimes g)^{\dagger}}

The inner square commutes because
f
and
g
are unitary maps.
Similarly, using
[U.5(b)]
, one can show that if
f
and
g
are unitary, then
f\oplus g
is unitary.

(3)

The proof is trivial.

5.2.
Unitary categories

With the notion of unitary objects in place, one can consider
\dagger
-isomix categories in which all the objects are unitary: these are called
unitary categories
. This section develops the theory of unitary categories.

{defi}

A
unitary category
is a
\dagger
-isomix category with unitary structure such that every object in the category is a unitary object.

Clearly, a unitary category must be a compact
\dagger
-LDC, because every object is in the core.

A
\dagger
-monoidal category is a strict unitary category in which the unitary structure map and the mix map are identity morphisms. Similarily, a
\dagger
-compact closed category is a strict unitary category in which all objects have unitary duals.

In the rest of this subsection, we show that any unitary category is
\dagger
-linearly equivalent to a conventional dagger monoidal category. A unitary category being a compact LDC is linearly equivalent, using
{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}:(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\oplus)
(see Corollary
4
) to the underlying monoidal category based on the par (and the tensor). We now show that for a unitary category one can induce a stationary on objects dagger on
(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\oplus)
. We denote this dagger by
(\_)^{\ddagger}
and define it by
f^{\ddagger}:=\varphi_{B}f^{\dagger}\varphi_{A}^{-1}
as illustrated by the left diagram below:

\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{B}}
\scriptstyle{f^{\ddagger}}
\scriptstyle{:=}
\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\textstyle{B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}}

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\scriptstyle{f^{\ddagger\ddagger}}
\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{B}}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\varphi_{A}^{-1})^{\dagger}}
\scriptstyle{(f^{\ddagger})^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

This new dagger clearly preserves composition and is also a stationary on objects involution as proven by the second diagram:
the lower square of this diagram is the dagger of the inverted definition and the resulting outer square is the naturality of
\iota
forcing
f^{\ddagger\ddagger}=f
.

Next, we observe that
u:X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}Y
is a unitary isomorphism in
\mathbb{X}
if and only if
u^{-1}=u^{\ddagger}
. This makes unitary isomorphisms in the traditional sense of categorical quantum mechanics coincide
with the notion introduced here. Thus,
u
is unitary in the sense here if and only if the diagram below commutes

\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\scriptstyle{u^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{A}

but this diagram commutes if and only if
u^{-1}=u^{\ddagger}
.

{defi}

A
\dagger

(1)

for all unitary objects

\varphi_{F(A)}=F(\varphi_{A})\rho^{F}

113.0001pt\raise-16.49501pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-2.71446pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{m_{\top}^{\dagger}}$}}}\kern Notice that if
F
preserves unitary structure, it must be an isomix functor by Lemma
11
. Also, when
A\in\mathbb{X}
is a unitary object, then
F(A)
must be a unitary object, and so
F(A)
is in the core.

We now show that
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}:(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\oplus)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
provides a unitary structure preserving equivalence of a dagger monoidal category into a unitary category:

Proposition 38
.

Unitary categories are
\dagger
-linearly equivalent via the mix functor
{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}:(\mathbb{X},\oplus,\oplus)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(\mathbb{X},\otimes,\oplus)
to the underlying dagger monoidal category on the par.
Furthermore, closed unitary categories under this equivalence become dagger compact closed categories.

Proof 5.6
.

We must exhibit a preservator, that is a natural transformation showing that the involution is preserved:

A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.43474pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits_{\hbox{\scriptsize$\varphi_{A}$}}}A^{\dagger}{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}(A^{\ddagger})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.43474pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\varphi_{A}$}}}{\sf Mx}_{\uparrow}(A)^{\dagger}

Note that
\varphi
is a natural transformation by the definition of
(\_)^{\ddagger}
and its coherence requirements
make it a linear natural equivalence. Making this the preservator immediately means that unitary structure is preserved.

Finally, we must show that unitary linear duals under
{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}
become
\ddagger
-duals. Given
(\eta,\epsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\!\dashv_{u}B
we must
show that under
{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}
this produces a dagger dual.
{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}(\eta)={\sf m}~\eta:\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus B
and

{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}(\epsilon)={\sf mx}^{-1}\epsilon:B\oplus A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot

We then require that
c_{\oplus}{\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}(\epsilon)={\sf Mx}^{*}_{\uparrow}(\eta)^{\ddagger}
. This is provided by:

\textstyle{A\oplus B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{{\sf mx}^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A\oplus B}}
\scriptstyle{c_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{B\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

5.3.
The unitary construction

A
\dagger
-isomix category can have many different unitary structures, as we shall describe in this section,
thus it is
structure
, and not a property. The requirements, however, do mean that for a
\dagger
-isomix category,
\mathbb{X}
, there is always the
smallest unitary structure, referred to as the “trivial” unitary structure, that produces a full unitary subcategory in
\mathbb{X}
. In this subsection, we provide a construction that produces this unitary category from any
\dagger
-isomix category. This construction, which we call the
unitary construction
provides an important technique for building unitary categories. The construction is based on identifying objects with pre-unitary structure: the tensor units always have a canonical pre-unitary structure so the construction always produces a non-empty category. However, to ensure that an application of the construction yields a unitary category in which there are objects which are not isomorphic to the units, one must exhibit concretely such objects. Fortunately this is often not difficult to do, making the construction quite applicable.

{defi}

(1)

In a
\dagger
-isomix category, a
pre-unitary object
is an object
U\in\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
, together with an isomorphism
\alpha:U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U^{\dagger}
such that
\alpha(\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger}=\iota
.

(2)

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
is a
\dagger
-isomix category, then define
{\sf Unitary}(\mathbb{X})
, the
unitary core
of
\mathbb{X}
, as follows:

Objects:

Pre-unitary objects
(U,\alpha)
,

Maps:

(U,\alpha)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.68407pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f$}}}(V,\beta)
where
U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.68407pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f$}}}V
is any map of
\mathbb{X}
.

We note that any object which is isomorphic to a preunitary object is also pre-unitary:

Lemma 39
.

In a
\dagger
-isomix category, if
U
is a pre-unitary object
and there exists an isomorphism
f:U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U^{\prime}
, then
U^{\prime}
is pre-unitary.

Our objective is to show that Unitary(
\mathbb{X}
) is endowed with all the structure of a unitary category.

Lemma 40
.

For any
\dagger
-isomix category, its canonical unitary core is a compact
\dagger
-LDC with tensor and par defined by

(\top,{\sf m}^{-1}\lambda_{\bot}:\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\top^{\dagger})~~~~~(A,\alpha)\otimes(B,\beta):=(A\otimes B,\mathsf{mx}(\alpha\oplus\beta)\lambda_{\oplus}:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A\otimes B)^{\dagger})

(\bot,{\sf m}~\lambda_{\top}:\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot^{\dagger})~~~~~(A,\alpha)\oplus(B,\beta):=(A\oplus B,\mathsf{mx}^{-1}(\alpha\otimes\beta)\lambda_{\otimes}:A\oplus B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A\oplus B)^{\dagger})

and
(U,\alpha)^{\dagger}:=(U^{\dagger},(\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger})
.

Proof 5.7
.

The proof uses the techniques of Lemma
33
.

Note that, as the map and tensor structure is inherited from
\mathbb{X}
, it suffices to show that these objects are all pre-unitary objects. Starting with
(U\alpha)^{\dagger}

we have:

(\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger}(((\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger})^{-1})^{\dagger}=(\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger}(\alpha^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=(\alpha^{\dagger}\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger}=(\iota^{-1})^{\dagger}=\iota

For the tensor and par we have:

\displaystyle{\sf m}^{-1}\lambda_{\bot}(({\sf m}^{-1}\lambda_{\bot})^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle={\sf m}^{-1}\lambda_{\bot}{\sf m}^{\dagger}\lambda_{\bot}^{\dagger}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny{\bf[$\dagger$-mix]}}}}{{=}}{\sf m}^{-1}{\sf m}\lambda_{\top}\lambda_{\bot}^{\dagger}=\iota

\displaystyle\mathsf{mx}^{-1}(\alpha\oplus\beta)\lambda_{\oplus}((\mathsf{mx}^{-1}(\alpha\oplus\beta)\lambda_{\oplus})^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{mx}^{-1}(\alpha\oplus\beta)\lambda_{\oplus}(\mathsf{mx}^{\dagger})(\alpha^{-1}\oplus\beta^{-1})^{\dagger}(\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{mx}^{-1}(\alpha\oplus\beta)\mathsf{mx}\lambda_{\otimes}(\alpha^{-1}\oplus\beta^{-1})^{\dagger}(\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=(\alpha\otimes\beta)\lambda_{\otimes}(\alpha^{-1}\oplus\beta^{-1})^{\dagger}(\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=(\alpha\otimes\beta)((\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\beta^{-1})^{\dagger})\lambda_{\otimes}(\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny{\bf Defn \ref{defn: pre-unitary}-(i)}}}}{{=}}(\iota\otimes\iota)\lambda_{\otimes}(\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny{\bf[$\dagger$-ldc.4]}}}}{{=}}\iota

\displaystyle{\sf m}\lambda_{\top}(({\sf m}\lambda_{\top})^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle={\sf m}\lambda_{\top}({\sf m}^{-1})^{\dagger}(\lambda_{\top}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle={\sf m}~{\sf m}^{-1}\lambda_{\bot}(\lambda_{\top}^{-1})^{\dagger}=\iota

\displaystyle\mathsf{mx}(\alpha\otimes\beta)\lambda_{\otimes}((\mathsf{mx}(\alpha\otimes\beta)\lambda_{\otimes})^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{mx}(\alpha\otimes\beta)\lambda_{\otimes}(\mathsf{mx}^{-1})^{\dagger}(\alpha^{-1}\otimes\beta^{-1})^{\dagger}(\lambda_{\otimes}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=(\alpha\oplus\beta)\mathsf{mx}~\mathsf{mx}^{-1}\lambda_{\oplus}(\alpha^{-1}\otimes\beta^{-1})^{\dagger}(\lambda_{\otimes}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=(\alpha\oplus\beta)((\alpha^{-1})^{\dagger}\oplus(\beta^{-1})^{\dagger})\lambda_{\oplus}(\lambda_{\otimes}^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=(\iota\oplus\iota)\lambda_{\oplus}(\lambda_{\otimes}^{-1})^{\dagger}=\iota

This makes
\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})
into a compact
\dagger
-LDC with all the structure inherited directly from
\mathbb{X}
.
However, more is true: each object now has an obvious unitary structure. This gives:

Proposition 41
.

For any
\dagger
-isomix category,
\mathbb{X}
,
\mathsf{Unitary}(\mathbb{X})
is a unitary category with a full and faithful underlying
\dagger
-isomix functor
U:{\sf Unitary}(\mathbb{X})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
.

Proof 5.8
.

The laxors are all identity maps so that the underlying functors is immediately a
\dagger
-mix functor.

It remains to show that every object is unitary: we set the unitary structure of an object to be
\alpha:(X,\alpha)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(X,\alpha)^{\dagger}
. However,
[U.1]
–
[U.5]
are immediately satisfied by construction implying this provides unitary structure for every object.

Next, we prove the couniversal property of the unitary construction. Define
{\sf UCat}
to be the category of unitary categories and
\dagger
-isomix functors that preserve unitary structure in the sense of Definition
5.2
, thus, whenever
{\varphi_{A}}
is the unitary structure then
F^{\prime}(\varphi_{A})\rho^{F^{\prime}}
is unitary structure. Define
Kompact
to be the category of compact
\dagger
-LDCs and
\dagger
-isomix functors.

We now show that the unitary construction produces a right adjoint to the underlying functor
U:{\sf UCat}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf Kompact}
which is the identity functor. Preliminary to this result we prove that Frobenius functors preserve preunitary objects:

Lemma 42
.

If
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
is a
\dagger
-isomix functor between compact
\dagger
-LDCs and
(A,\varphi)
is a preunitary object of
\mathbb{X}
, then
(F(A),F(\varphi)\rho)
is a preunitary object of
\mathbb{Y}
.

Proof 5.9
.

To prove that
(F(A),F(\varphi)\rho)
is a preunitary object, one has the following computation:

\displaystyle F(\varphi)\rho((F(\varphi)\rho)^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=F(\varphi)\rho F(\varphi^{-1})^{\dagger}(\rho^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=F(\varphi(\varphi^{-1})^{\dagger})\rho(\rho^{-1})^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=F(\iota)\rho(\rho^{-1})^{\dagger}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\bf[\dagger-isomix]}}}{{=}}\iota

Proposition 43
.

U:{\sf UCat}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf Kompact}
has a right adjoint
{\sf Unitary}:{\sf Kompact}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}{\sf UCat};\mathbb{C}\mapsto{\sf Unitary}(\mathbb{C})
.

Proof 5.10
.

The couniversal diagram is as follows:

\textstyle{U(\mathbb{U})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F}
\scriptstyle{U(F^{\flat})}
\textstyle{\mathbb{C}}
\textstyle{U({\sf Unitary}(\mathbb{C}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\epsilon}

Since
F
is a
\dagger
-isomix functor it preserves preunitary structure (see Lemma
42
). This means that each
(U,\varphi_{U})
in
\mathbb{U}
is carried by
F
onto a preunitary object in
\mathbb{C}
,
(F(U),F(\varphi)\rho^{F})
. But a preunitary object in
\mathbb{C}
is an object of
{\sf Unitary}(\mathbb{C})
and this determines
F^{\flat}
. The functor
F^{\flat}
is uniquely determined as it must preserve the unitary structure.

5.4.
Examples of unitary constructions

In Section
4
, we discussed examples of
\dagger
-isomix categories in which the
\dagger
is given by composing the conjugation functor and the dualizing functor. In the rest of the section, we apply the unitary construction to each of those examples to construct a unitary category:

5.4.1.
Category of abstract state spaces

In Section
3.5.3
, we discussed a construction on a
\dagger
-isomix category,
\mathbb{X}
, that produces a category of abstract state spaces,
\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
, which is a
\dagger
-isomix category. In this section, we examine the preunitary objects of
\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
. Since all the basic natural isomorphisms are inherited from
\mathbb{X}
,
\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{X})
determine
\mathsf{Core}(\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X}))
. If
(A,\alpha)
is a preunitary object for
\mathbb{X}
, and
(A,e_{A},u_{A})\in\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
then,
((A,e_{A},u_{A}),\alpha)
is a preunitary object for
\mathsf{Asp}(\mathbb{X})
if
u_{A}\alpha=\lambda_{\top}e_{A}^{\dagger}
.

5.4.2.
Category of a group with involution

We discussed a source of examples of compact
\dagger
-LDCs which are given by groups with conjugation. Applying unitary construction to each of the example categories results in the following unitary categories. It could be noticed that the preunitary objects in each of these categories includes those group elements such that
\overline{g^{-1}}=g
. More explicitly, the preunitary objects are
(g,1)
such that
\overline{g^{-1}}=g
.

•

In the discrete category of complex numbers,
\mathbb{D}(\mathbb{C},+,0)
,

(a+ib)^{\dagger}:=\overline{(a+ib)^{*}}=\overline{(-a-ib)}=-a+ib

The preunitary objects in this category are given by all complex numbers, i.e.,
(ib,1)
.

•

In the discrete category of non-zero complex numbers,
\mathbb{D}(\mathbb{C},.,1)
, the preunitary objects are given by complex numbers on a unit circle.

•

In the discrete category,
\mathbb{D}(P(x),+,0)
, where
P(x)
is a polynomial ring,
P(x)^{\dagger}=-P(-x)
and the preunitary objects are polynomials
P(x)=\sum_{n}a_{n}x^{n}
such that n is odd.

•

In
\mathbb{D}(\mathbb{M}_{2},\cdot,I_{2})
where
\mathbb{M}_{2}
is the group of
2\times 2
invertible matrices over
\mathbb{C}
. The
\dagger
structure is as follows:

\left(\begin{matrix}a+ib&m+in\\
c+id&p+iq\end{matrix}\right)^{\dagger}:=\overline{\left(\begin{matrix}a+ib&m+in\\
c+id&p+iq\end{matrix}\right)^{*}}=\left(\begin{matrix}a-ib&c-id\\
m-in&p-iq\end{matrix}\right)^{-1}

The preunitary objects in this category are given by unitary matrices.

5.4.3.
Category of Hopf Modules in a
*
-autonomous category

In Section
4.4.3
, we described a construction of
\dagger
-isomix categories from any symmetric isomix
*
-autonomous category,
\mathbb{X}
, by choosing the Hopf Modules over a cocommutative
\otimes
-Hopf Algebra. We referred to the resulting category as
{\mbox{\bf H-Mod}}_{\mathbb{X}}
. Now we shall look at the preunitary objects in
{\mbox{\bf H-Mod}}_{\mathbb{X}}
in order to apply the unitary construction to this category. We begin by identifying the objects in the core of
{\mbox{\bf H-Mod}}_{\mathbb{X}}
:

.

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
is a mix

is a cocommutative Hopf Algebra in
\mathbb{X}
. If
